request-lifecycle.title: How a Request Travels
request-lifecycle.summary: Follow one page load hop by hop — and find out where the time really goes.

goals.text: What DNS does and why it is cached
Why a connection costs round trips
The path: browser → server → database → back
Cases: a slow query and a distant user

steps.title: Users say the shop feels slow
body: Before you can make something faster, you need to know where the time goes. So let’s follow a single page load.
You type shop.example and press Enter. About a sixth of a second later the page appears. A lot happens in between.

callout.text: Every web request is a conversation between machines. Each step costs time, and the costs add up.

steps.title: Find the address (DNS)
body: Networks route by numeric IP address, not by name. So the browser first asks a DNS resolver: where is shop.example?
The answer — 203.0.113.7 — comes back in about 20 ms.

callout.text: Answers are cached for a time-to-live (TTL). For the next few minutes, repeat visits skip this step entirely.

steps.title: Open a connection
body: Now the browser opens a connection to 203.0.113.7. A TCP handshake agrees to talk; a TLS handshake sets up encryption. Each needs a round trip — there and back.
Here a round trip takes 30 ms, so connecting costs 60 ms before a single byte of the page is requested.

callout.text: Round-trip time (RTT) is set by distance and the network, not by how fast your server is.

steps.title: Send the request
body: Over the open connection the browser sends GET /products. The server parses it, checks the session and runs your code.
That costs one more round trip plus ~10 ms of server work.
changes: + Request: 1 round trip + 10 ms server time

steps.title: The server asks the database
body: The products don’t live in the web server — they live in a database. The server sends a query and waits for the rows to come back.
Watch a request travel all the way in and the response all the way out.

callout.text: Keeping the server stateless and the data in a database is what later lets us run many servers. (See Scaling.)

steps.title: The response comes home
body: The server turns rows into HTML and sends it back; downloading it takes another 20 ms. The browser renders the page — 155 ms after you pressed Enter.
Then it notices images and stylesheets in the page and fires off more requests. Reusing the open connection saves them the handshake.

steps.title: One page, forty more requests
body: The HTML is only the start. It references images, stylesheets, scripts and fonts — about 40 more files — and the browser fetches them all.
With old HTTP/1.1 each connection carried one request at a time, so browsers opened ~6 connections and queued the rest. HTTP/2 sends them all at once over the single connection we already opened.

callout.text: Fewer, smaller files still help: bundle scripts, compress text (gzip/brotli), use modern image formats, and lazy-load what’s below the fold.

changes: + 40 more requests: images, CSS, JS, fonts
~ All multiplexed over one HTTP/2 connection

steps.title: Case: one slow query
body: A new “recommended for you” box ships. Its query sorts every product by a score on each page view, and the database now takes 400 ms to answer.
Same network, same handshakes — but the page jumps from 155 ms to over half a second. Watch requests wait at the database.

callout.text: Measure before optimising. Here the network is fine; the fix is in the database (see the Indexes lesson).

steps.title: Case: a user in Sydney
body: Back to the fast query. Now the same page is opened in Sydney, while the server is in Virginia: every round trip takes about 200 ms instead of 30.
Two handshake round trips plus the request round trip cost 600 ms before the page even downloads. Same server, same code — over 4× slower.

callout.text: Cut round trips (TLS 1.3, HTTP/3, keep connections open) and move content closer to users (CDNs, regions — Module 02).

changes: ~ User in Sydney · 200 ms per round trip

steps.title: Where the time went
body: Of 155 ms, only about 25 ms was the server and database actually working. The other ~130 ms was messages crossing the network.

• DNS turns names into addresses; answers are cached.
  • Connections cost round trips — reuse them.
  • Server code is often the smallest slice of latency — unless a slow query sneaks in.
  • Distance multiplies every round trip.

callout.text: Next up: Latency & Throughput — what happens to that 155 ms when thousands of users arrive at once.

sum.title: Where the time went
lines: # 130 ms of it is waiting on the network

latency-throughput.title: Latency & Throughput
latency-throughput.summary: Two questions about speed — and why busy servers slow down before they’re full.

goals.text: Why distance sets a latency floor
Little’s Law, fan-out tails and batching

steps.title: Two different questions
body: Latency: how long does one request take, from leaving the user to the answer coming back? Watch one dot go out and return.
Throughput: how many requests does the system finish per second? Count the dots.

callout.text: Think of a highway: latency is how long your drive takes; throughput is how many cars pass per hour. Extra lanes let more cars through, but on an empty road they don’t get you there any sooner.

steps.title: More users, same server
body: Traffic grows 7×. Throughput climbs with it — the server is still keeping up — and it’s now 70% busy: 350 of the roughly 500 req/s it can handle.
But look at the line in front of it: requests occasionally have to wait their turn. Waiting is latency too.

callout.text: Utilization = the fraction of time the server is busy. At 70%, a new request often finds it already working on something.

steps.title: The hockey stick
body: Traffic grows by another third and the server hits 96% busy. Throughput only rises to 480 req/s — a whisker under its ceiling of 500 — but the queue explodes and latency goes up sevenfold.
Requests don’t arrive evenly spaced. With 30% spare, a burst is absorbed quickly; with 4% spare, each burst piles up behind requests that are already waiting, and the line takes ages to clear.

callout.text: Latency grows slowly, then suddenly. Plan to run around 60–70% busy at peak and keep the rest as headroom.

steps.title: Averages hide the pain
body: Back at 70% busy, most requests are quick — but a few get stuck behind slow work. The average here is about 180 ms, which looks healthy: it blends the slow few away.
So we measure percentiles: p50 is the time half of requests beat; p99 is the time only 1 in 100 exceeds.

callout.text: A page that makes 30 requests hits the p99 on about 1 load in 4 (1 − 0.99³⁰ ≈ 26%). Tail latency is what users actually feel.

steps.title: Add capacity, buy back latency
body: Double the server’s cores and the same 350 req/s is now only 35% of its capacity. The queue drains and both p50 and p99 fall.
Throughput didn’t change — demand didn’t change. What changed is how much headroom there is to absorb bursts.

callout.text: To lower latency under load, lower utilization: more capacity, or less work per request.

steps.title: Distance is latency too
body: Now move the server across an ocean. Nothing about it got slower, yet every round trip takes longer — watch the dots travel.
Light in fiber covers about 200 km per millisecond. New York ↔ London is ~5,600 km: at least 56 ms per round trip, closer to 75 ms in practice.

callout.text: No server upgrade beats physics. To cut this latency, move the data closer to users (caches, CDNs, regions).

steps.title: Little’s Law: how much is in flight
body: A simple rule ties the numbers together: requests in flight = throughput × latency. At 350 req/s and 0.12 s each, about 42 requests are being worked on at any moment.
Each in-flight request holds a thread, a connection or some memory. If latency rises to 1 s at the same throughput, 350 are in flight — and pools sized for 50 run dry.

callout.text: Use it to size thread pools, connection pools and worker counts — and to see why slow dependencies exhaust them.

steps.title: One request, many servers
body: A search page asks 100 index servers in parallel and must wait for the slowest. Each server is quick 99% of the time — but with 100 of them, a page usually hits at least one slow one.
1 − 0.99¹⁰⁰ ≈ 63% of searches wait on someone’s p99. A rare tail on one server becomes the common case for the whole page.

callout.text: Fix the tail with hedged requests: if a server hasn’t answered by its p95, send the same request to a replica and take whichever answers first.

changes: ~ p99 of one server → typical page

chart.title: Waiting for the slowest
lines: each server slow 1% of the time

steps.title: Batching: more throughput, a bit more latency
body: Writing analytics events one row at a time, the database manages about 2,000 inserts per second — most of the cost is per-statement overhead.
Group them: collect events for up to 50 ms and write 100 rows in one statement (the big squares). Throughput jumps 25×, while each event waits up to 50 ms longer.

callout.text: Batching trades latency for throughput. Great for logs, analytics and bulk imports; wrong for a user waiting on a click.

steps.title: Recap
body:
• Latency is time per request; throughput is requests per second.
  • Latency explodes as utilization nears 100% — keep headroom.
  • Watch p99, not the average: the tail is what users feel.
  • Distance adds latency no server can remove.
  • In flight = throughput × latency; fan-out turns rare tails into common ones.

callout.text: Next up: Napkin Math — estimating how much capacity you need before you build anything.

napkin-math.title: Napkin Math
napkin-math.summary: Turn a product idea into servers and terabytes with math that fits on a napkin.

goals.text: Size for the peak, not the average

steps.title: Will one server do?
body: You’re designing PhotoShare. Before choosing any technology you need a sense of scale: is this one server, or a hundred?
You don’t need exact numbers — just the right order of magnitude. Napkin math gets you there in minutes.

callout.text: Interviewers and architects both start here: rough numbers first, then design to fit them.

card.title: The brief
lines: they upload **1M** photos a day, 2 MB each
# Will one server cope? How much storage?

steps.title: Daily users → requests per second
body: Start from what you know: users and how often they act. 10M users × 20 requests = 200M requests a day.
A day has 86,400 seconds. Round it to 100,000 — napkin math is about being quick, not precise.

callout.text: Handy shortcut: 1M requests per day ≈ 12 requests per second.

steps.title: Plan for the peak, not the average
body: Traffic isn’t flat: people browse in the evening and around big events. A typical peak is 2–3× the daily average.
Size for 3× and the lone server is clearly overwhelmed.

callout.text: A system sized for its average load is down at exactly the moment most people use it.

steps.title: How many servers?
body: A load test shows one server handles about 1,000 req/s. Peak is 7,000, so we need 7 — plus headroom for spikes and for a server failing.
Call it 10. Notice we used a measured number, not a guess.

callout.text: Spreading traffic across these servers is the job of a load balancer — see Module 02.

steps.title: How much storage?
body: Photos are the big one: 1M uploads × 2 MB = 2 TB per day. Over a year that’s ~730 TB.
Data is usually stored three times so a dead disk loses nothing — so plan for about 2 PB in year one. That rules out “one database server” immediately.

callout.text: Storage grows every day and never resets. Requests per second come and go; bytes stay.

card.title: Storage
lines: = plan for ~2 PB in year one

steps.title: How much network?
body: Uploads are the small part: 2 TB a day is about 20 MB/s coming in. Viewing is the big part: if each user looks at 100 photos a day as 200 KB thumbnails, that’s 200 TB a day going out.
200 TB ÷ 100,000 s ≈ 2 GB/s — about 16 Gbit/s on average, more at peak. That’s a job for a CDN, not ten web servers.

callout.text: Read-heavy media apps are usually limited by bandwidth before CPU. Estimate bytes out, not just requests.

steps.title: Will it fit in memory?
body: Feeds read photo metadata and user profiles constantly. Could a cache hold the hot part? Profiles: 10M × 2 KB = 20 GB. Today’s new photos: 1M × 1 KB = 1 GB.
About 21 GB — it fits in the memory of a single cache server (with a second for redundancy). No exotic architecture needed.

callout.text: Napkin math often says “this is smaller than you think”. That’s just as valuable as finding something big.

steps.title: Numbers worth memorising
body: A handful of numbers make most estimates possible. Learn the orders of magnitude, not the decimals.

Read from memory100 ns
Read from SSD100 µs
Round trip, same data center0.5 ms
Round trip, across an ocean75–150 ms
Seconds in a day~100,000

steps.title: Recap
body:
• Users × actions ÷ 100k s gives average requests per second.
  • Multiply by 2–3× for the peak, and size for that.
  • Servers = peak ÷ per-server capacity, plus headroom.
  • Storage = items/day × size × 365 × copies.
  • Estimate bytes out and memory too — they often decide the design.

callout.text: That finishes Foundations. Next: Vertical vs Horizontal Scaling — what to do when the numbers say one machine won’t do.

vertical-horizontal.title: Vertical vs Horizontal Scaling
vertical-horizontal.summary: Your one server is melting. Do you buy a bigger one, or more of them?

goals.text: Spot the symptoms of an overloaded server
Scale up — and know its limits
Scale out with many smaller servers
Autoscale with the daily cycle — and pre-scale for spikes
See why scaling out needs a load balancer

steps.title: It starts with one server
body: Your app runs on a single machine. Every request — opening a page, posting a photo — travels from a user’s device to that server and back.
With a hundred users it barely notices: the CPU idles around 1%.

callout.text: A server has a fixed budget of CPU, memory, disk and network. Its capacity is how many requests per second it can serve before one of those runs out.

steps.title: Then you go viral
body: A post takes off and traffic jumps 120×. This machine can serve about 400 requests per second, and 480 are arriving. The CPU pins at 100%, requests queue up waiting their turn, latency balloons, and some give up and time out.
You need more capacity. There are two fundamentally different ways to get it.

callout.text: Overload looks like: CPU near 100%, growing request queues, rising latency, then timeouts.

steps.title: Way 1 — scale up
body: The simplest fix: move to a bigger machine. More cores, more memory, faster disks.
Nothing about your design changes — the code doesn’t even know. This is vertical scaling, or scaling up.

callout.text: Scaling up is a great first move: zero code changes and nothing new to operate. Four times the machine, roughly four times the price.

steps.title: …until you hit the ceiling
body: Growth continues and you upgrade again and again — but machines only get so big. Even the largest general-purpose server can’t keep up, and software rarely uses 192 cores as well as it used 16: locks, memory and one shared disk get in the way.
Every upgrade is also a migration: a restart, and downtime while you move.

callout.text: Vertical scaling has a hard ceiling. In the cloud, price grows roughly in line with size — until the top of the range, where the exotic machines carry a premium and twice the cores no longer means twice the throughput.

steps.title: …and it’s a single point of failure
body: Worse, everything depends on one machine. A bad deploy, a full disk or a dead power supply and the whole product is offline.
A component whose failure takes the entire system down is a single point of failure (SPOF).

callout.text: However big it is, one box is always one failure away from a full outage.

steps.title: Way 2 — scale out
body: Instead of one giant machine, run several mid-size ones side by side — here four with 96 vCPU each — all running the same code.

Need more capacity? Add another server. Mid-size machines are the best value, there’s no hard ceiling, and each one is a small slice of the whole. This is horizontal scaling, or scaling out — how virtually every large system grows.

callout.text: Four 96-vCPU servers have twice the capacity of the biggest single machine — and any one of them can fail while the other three carry the load.

steps.title: Peak capacity, idle all night
body: Traffic follows the clock. At 8 p.m. you need all four servers; at 4 a.m. traffic is a tenth of that, and they sit at 5% CPU.
You’re paying for peak capacity 24 hours a day. Most of the time, most of it does nothing.

callout.text: Consumer apps commonly swing 3–10× between their daily peak and trough.

steps.title: Autoscaling: follow the demand
body: Because the servers are interchangeable, an autoscaler can add and remove them automatically — for example, keep average CPU near 50%.
At night it scales in to two servers — never fewer, so one can still fail — and in the evening it scales back out. You pay roughly for what you use.

callout.text: Autoscaling only works when servers are stateless and sit behind a load balancer — the next two lessons.

changes: ~ CPU 5% → 10% on the two that remain

steps.title: Case: the flash sale
body: At noon two servers are comfortably serving 150,000 users. Then a flash sale starts and traffic jumps 5× in two minutes. The autoscaler reacts — but a new server takes about three minutes to boot and warm up.

For those minutes the two running servers can serve only about two-thirds of the traffic. The fix is to scale before the spike: scheduled scaling for known events, and spare headroom for unknown ones.

callout.text: Autoscaling reacts; it can’t predict. Pre-warm for launches, sales and big broadcasts.

steps.title: But who sends users where?
body: Right now each group of users is hard-wired to one server’s address. When Server B dies, a quarter of your users get errors — even though three healthy servers are right there.
Clients can’t tell which servers are alive or busy. Something has to sit in front and steer every request to a healthy server.

callout.text: That something is a load balancer — the subject of the next lesson.

steps.title: Recap: up vs out
body:
Scale upScale out
HowBigger machineMore machines
Code changesNoneSome1
CeilingHardware limitPractically none
FailureTotal outagePartial2
To growMigrate + restartAdd a server
CostPremium at the topLinear
Scaling out also lets you autoscale: add servers for the evening peak, remove them at night.
1 Servers must be interchangeable — see Stateless Services. 2 Zero, once a load balancer routes around failures.

callout.text: Rule of thumb: scale up while it’s cheap and simple, then scale out.

load-balancing.title: Load Balancing
load-balancing.summary: One front door for many servers — and the rules for who gets which request.

goals.text: Why a pool of servers needs one front door
Health checks that route around failure
Removing the load balancer as a SPOF

steps.title: Three servers, one address
body: We scaled out to three servers — but users only know one address, the one in DNS. Every request lands on Server B while A and C sit idle.
The extra hardware bought us nothing. We need a single front door that spreads requests across all of them.

callout.text: Adding servers only helps if traffic actually reaches them.

steps.title: Put a load balancer in front
body: A load balancer (LB) becomes the one public address of the service. Clients connect to it; it forwards each request to one of the servers behind it and relays the answer back.
Servers can now come and go without clients ever knowing.

callout.text: The servers behind a load balancer are called its pool (or target group).

changes: ~ Users now talk to the LB, not to servers

steps.title: Round robin: take turns
body: How does the LB choose? The simplest rule is round robin: A, then B, then C, then A again. Watch the requests go out in turn.
It’s cheap and fair — as long as the servers are equally powerful and every request costs about the same.

callout.text: Weighted round robin gives bigger servers a bigger share, e.g. A : B : C = 2 : 1 : 1.

changes: ~ Slowed down so you can follow each request

steps.title: When requests aren’t equal
body: Real traffic is lumpy. Loading a page takes 5 ms; exporting a year of reports takes 5 seconds. Round robin counts requests, not work.
Here every third request is heavy (the big squares), and by luck of the rotation they all land on Server B. It drowns while A and C coast.

callout.text: Round robin has no idea how busy a server actually is.

steps.title: Least connections
body: With least connections, the LB tracks how many requests each server is busy with and sends the next one to the least busy.
A server stuck on slow work holds more open connections, so it automatically receives less new work. The load evens out.

callout.text: Other strategies: least response time, IP hash (same client → same server) and power of two choices (pick two at random, use the less busy).

steps.title: Health checks route around failure
body: Every few seconds the LB probes each server — say GET /health. A server that misses several checks in a row is pulled out of the pool; once it recovers, it’s put back.
Server C just crashed, and users didn’t notice a thing. In the last lesson, a dead server meant errors for a quarter of them.

callout.text: Health checks plus spare servers mean no single server is a single point of failure any more.

changes: ~ C taken out of the pool

steps.title: Who balances the balancer?
body: We removed one single point of failure and created another. Every request now passes through one load balancer — when it dies, so does everything behind it.
The servers are perfectly healthy. Nobody can reach them.

callout.text: Anything that every request depends on must itself be redundant.

steps.title: Add a standby
body: Run two load balancers: an active one serving traffic and a passive standby. They share a virtual IP (VIP) — the address clients actually use — and exchange heartbeats every second.

callout.text: Cloud load balancers (AWS ELB, Google Cloud LB…) do this for you: they run redundantly across machines and zones.

steps.title: Failover in seconds
body: The active LB dies. The standby notices the missing heartbeats, claims the virtual IP and starts forwarding traffic.
Clients keep using the same address. At worst, a few in-flight requests are retried.

callout.text: This pattern — active–passive failover — protects databases, caches and queues too.

changes: ~ VIP moved to the new active LB

steps.title: Route by what’s in the request
body: Load balancers come in two kinds. A layer 4 balancer only sees IP addresses and ports, and forwards whole connections. A layer 7 balancer reads the HTTP request itself.
That lets it route by path: /api/* to the API servers, /images/* to a separate image service — each pool scaled and deployed on its own.

callout.text: L7 balancers can also route by host name, header or cookie, terminate TLS, and add caching or compression.

steps.title: Case: deploying without downtime
body: Time to ship version 2. A rolling deploy updates one server at a time: the load balancer first drains it — no new requests, but in-flight ones finish — then it’s updated, passes its health check and rejoins.
Here C is already on v2, B is draining, and A waits its turn. Users never see an error.

callout.text: Blue-green deploys go further: bring up a full v2 pool, then switch the load balancer over at once — and back, if anything looks wrong.

steps.title: Recap
body:
• A load balancer gives a pool of servers one stable address.
  • Round robin is simple; least connections adapts to uneven work.
  • Health checks pull dead servers out of the pool automatically.
  • The LB must be redundant too: active–passive with a shared VIP.
  • L7 balancers route by path; draining enables zero-downtime deploys.

callout.text: Next up: Stateless Services — what breaks when a user’s next request lands on a different server.

stateless.title: Stateless Services
stateless.summary: Why the next request must work on any server — and where the state goes instead.

goals.text: What “state” is, and why it pins users to a server
Sticky sessions — and how they break
A shared session store makes servers interchangeable

steps.title: Alice logs in
body: Alice signs in and adds two things to her cart. Her request happened to land on Server A, which keeps a session in its memory: who she is and what’s in her cart.
Her browser holds a cookie with the session id, so later requests can find it again.

callout.text: State is anything a server remembers between requests: logins, carts, half-finished uploads.

steps.title: Her next request lands elsewhere
body: The load balancer is doing its job — round robin sends Alice’s next requests to B and then C. Neither has ever heard of her.
To Alice the app is broken: one page shows her cart, the next asks her to sign in again.

callout.text: If a server keeps state in memory, every other server is useless for that user.

changes: ~ Requests 2 and 3 go to B and C

steps.title: Fix 1: sticky sessions
body: Tell the load balancer to remember where each user started — usually with a cookie — and keep sending them there. Alice always reaches A, so she stays signed in.
Quick to switch on, and no code changes.

callout.text: Sticky users can’t be moved. If many of them pile onto one server, it stays overloaded while others idle.

steps.title: …until Server A dies
body: Server A crashes. The load balancer does the right thing and moves Alice to B — but her session died with A’s memory.
She’s signed out and her cart is empty. Every user pinned to A just had the same experience.

callout.text: Sticky sessions turn every server into a small single point of failure for its users.

steps.title: Fix 2: move the state out
body: Keep sessions in a shared, fast session store (often Redis). Every server reads Alice’s session from it, so any server can handle any request.
The servers are now stateless: they remember nothing between requests. Round robin is back, and she stays signed in.

callout.text: The cost: one extra hop of about a millisecond per request — cheap, for servers you can add, remove or lose freely.

steps.title: Now losing a server is a non-event
body: Server A dies again. The load balancer routes around it, B and C read the same session from the store, and Alice doesn’t notice.
This is what makes autoscaling possible: servers can be created and destroyed at any moment.

callout.text: Stateless servers are cattle, not pets — any one of them can be replaced without anyone noticing.

changes: ~ Alice still signed in, cart intact

steps.title: Or: let the request carry it
body: Another option is to put the state in the request itself: a signed token (such as a JWT) that says “this is Alice”. Any server can verify the signature without looking anything up.
No store and no extra hop — but a token can’t easily be cancelled before it expires, and it travels with every request, so keep it small.

callout.text: Common split: tokens for identity, a shared store for anything big or that must change instantly (carts, revoked logins).

steps.title: Case: files on a local disk
body: Alice uploads a new avatar. Server A saves avatar.png to its own disk and shows it — perfect.
Her next page loads from Server B, which has no such file: a broken image. Files are state too.

callout.text: Anything written to a server’s local disk — uploads, generated PDFs, temp files — disappears for every other server, and for good when the server is replaced.

changes: + Avatar saved on Server A’s disk
− Broken image when served by B or C

steps.title: Put files in object storage
body: Store files in shared object storage (Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob): effectively unlimited, durable, and reachable from every server.
Server A writes the avatar there (dark square); B and C read the same file. Better still, browsers fetch images straight from storage through a CDN.

callout.text: Rule of thumb: servers keep nothing that must outlive the request. Sessions → a store or token; files → object storage; data → the database.

changes: ~ Uploads written to storage, not local disk

steps.title: Recap
body:
• State kept in a server’s memory pins users to that server.
  • Sticky sessions hide the problem until a server dies.
  • Move state to a shared store, or carry it in a signed token.
  • Files go to object storage, never a server’s local disk.
  • Stateless servers can be added, removed and lost freely.

callout.text: Next up: Caching — the database behind all these stateless servers is about to become the bottleneck.

caching.title: Caching
caching.summary: Keep the answers people ask for most somewhere much faster than the database.

goals.text: Why the same reads overload a database
Why hit rate matters so much
Stampedes, missing keys and cache layers

steps.title: Every page hits the database
body: Your shop is popular. Every product page asks the database for the same kind of thing — name, price, photos — and it’s now 92% busy.
Reads queue up and pages slow to nearly half a second at p95.

callout.text: Databases are usually the hardest part to scale, because they hold the data. Protect them from unnecessary work.

steps.title: The same few things, over and over
body: Look at what’s actually being read: a small set of popular products accounts for most traffic. The database recomputes the same answers thousands of times a minute.
Answers that are read often and change rarely are perfect to keep somewhere closer and faster.

callout.text: Most real workloads are skewed like this — a few hot items and a long tail of rarely-read ones.

card.title: Who reads what
lines: # the same rows, read again and again

steps.title: Put a cache in front
body: Add an in-memory cache (such as Redis or Memcached). The server checks it first: a hit returns in about a millisecond.
On a miss (amber) the server reads the database, then saves a copy in the cache for next time. This is the cache-aside pattern.

callout.text: A cache lookup is one key fetched from memory: no query planning, no joins, no disk. It typically answers 10–100× faster than the query it replaces.

steps.title: Hit rate is everything
body: The share of reads answered by the cache is the hit rate. Because misses are so much slower, small changes in hit rate matter a lot.
Going from 80% to 95% hits more than halves the average read time and cuts database load by three-quarters.

callout.text: Raise hit rate by caching the right things, giving the cache enough memory, and keeping entries long enough to be reused.

steps.title: The price changed. The cache didn’t.
body: An admin updates a price from $20 to $25. The database has the new price — but the cache still holds the old copy, and that’s what users see.
A cache is a second copy of the truth. Keeping copies in sync is the hard part of caching.

callout.text: “There are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things.” — Phil Karlton

steps.title: Invalidate on write, expire with a TTL
body: When data changes, the server writes the database and deletes the cached copy (red rings). The next read misses and fetches the fresh value.
As a safety net, every entry also gets a TTL (time to live): even if an invalidation is missed, stale data disappears within a minute.
Why delete rather than overwrite the cached copy? Two writes racing each other can leave the older value in the cache. Deleting is always safe: the next read reloads the truth.

callout.text: Pick the TTL by asking: how stale is acceptable? Seconds for prices and stock, hours for a product description.

steps.title: Memory runs out
body: The cache can’t hold everything — memory is expensive. When it’s full, something has to go to make room.
The usual rule is LRU: evict the entry that was least recently used. Hot items stay; the long tail cycles through.
The main alternative, LFU, evicts the least frequently used entry instead — better when a burst of one-off reads would otherwise push out the real favourites.

callout.text: A cache only needs to hold the hot set. 10% of the data can easily serve 90% of reads.

steps.title: Case: the cache stampede
body: The home page is the hottest key in the cache — 2,000 reads a second. Its TTL expires. In the next instant, every one of those requests misses and goes to the database for the same answer.
The database, used to 8% load, gets hit by a wall of identical queries and stalls. This is a cache stampede (or thundering herd).

callout.text: The more popular a key, the more dangerous its expiry.

steps.title: Let one request refill it
body: Fix it with request coalescing: the first miss takes a short lock and fetches from the database; everyone else waits a few milliseconds for that one result.
Add two more habits: refresh hot keys a little before they expire, and add random jitter to TTLs so many keys don’t expire at the same moment.

callout.text: Libraries call this “single-flight”. CDNs do the same at the edge (“request collapsing”).

steps.title: Case: asking for what isn’t there
body: A crawler — or an attacker — requests product IDs that don’t exist: /product/99900017, …18, …19. Each one misses the cache, goes to the database, finds nothing, and so leaves nothing to cache.
Every such request is a guaranteed miss, however often it repeats. The cache gives no protection at all, and the database is busy searching for rows that were never there. This is cache penetration.

callout.text: Cache-aside only remembers answers. “No such row” is an answer too — if you forget to store it, you pay for it every time.

changes: + Requests for IDs that don’t exist
~ Half of all reads now miss

users.label: real users + a crawler guessing IDs

steps.title: Remember the “no” as well
body: First fix: negative caching. Store “not found” in the cache too, with a short TTL, so a repeated request for the same missing ID stops at the cache.

But a crawler never repeats itself. For that, keep a Bloom filter of every real ID in the server’s memory: a compact bit set that answers “definitely not here” or “probably here” in microseconds. Impossible IDs get a 404 without touching the cache or the database.

callout.text: A Bloom filter never says “no” to a key that exists; it occasionally says “maybe” to one that doesn’t. A 1% false-positive rate costs only about 10 bits per key.

changes: + Bloom filter of real IDs on the server

users.label: real users + a crawler guessing IDs

card.title: Bloom filter · 12 M IDs in 15 MB

steps.title: Caches everywhere
body: The cache we built is one layer of many. A request may be answered by the browser cache, the CDN, an in-process cache on the server, a shared cache like Redis, or the database’s own memory.
The closer to the user, the faster and cheaper the hit — and the harder it is to invalidate.

callout.text: Most of “making it fast” is deciding what can be cached, where, and for how long.

steps.title: Recap
body:
• Cache answers that are read often and change rarely.
  • Cache-aside: check the cache, fall back to the database, then fill the cache.
  • Hit rate drives both speed and database load.
  • Plan for staleness: invalidate on write, add a TTL, evict with LRU.
  • Protect hot keys from stampedes: one fetch, early refresh, jittered TTLs.
  • Cache “not found” too, and screen impossible keys with a Bloom filter.

callout.text: Next up: Content Delivery — caching files on servers spread around the world, close to your users.

cdn.title: Content Delivery
cdn.summary: Copy what everyone downloads to servers near your users — and stop fighting the speed of light.

goals.text: How edge servers cache static files
Cold caches and versioned file names
How a CDN shields the origin

steps.title: Your users are far away
body: Your servers are in Virginia. A user in London waits about 75 ms per round trip; in Sydney about 200 ms. A page needs many round trips, so Sydney waits well over a second.
Meanwhile every image for every user worldwide is served by that one origin.

callout.text: You can’t speed up light. The only way to cut distance latency is to serve users from somewhere closer.

steps.title: Most bytes are the same for everyone
body: Look inside a page load. The HTML is personal, but images, scripts, stylesheets and videos are identical for every user.
Identical, rarely-changing files are perfect for caching — anywhere, including far from the origin.

callout.text: Static assets are often 90%+ of the bytes on a page.

card.title: What a page is made of
lines: = 98% of bytes are the same for everyone

steps.title: Put copies at the edge
body: A CDN (content delivery network) runs edge servers in hundreds of cities. Point your static files at it, and each user is served by the edge nearest them.
London now gets images in ~10 ms. Only misses (amber) travel all the way to Virginia.

callout.text: Popular CDNs: Cloudflare, Fastly, Akamai, Amazon CloudFront. You rent their edges; you don’t run them.

changes: + Edge servers in London and Sydney
~ 90% of requests answered at the edge

steps.title: First requests are misses
body: Edges are pull-through caches: they start empty. The first request for a file misses, the edge fetches it from the origin, keeps a copy, and serves everyone after that.
London’s edge is warm; Sydney’s just started and is still filling up — so Sydney users briefly pay the long trip.

callout.text: This is the same cache-aside idea from the last lesson, spread around the planet.

changes: ~ Sydney edge: cold, filling from origin

steps.title: You ship a new logo. Nobody sees it.
body: You replace logo.png on the origin. But edges cached the old one with a one-day TTL, so users keep seeing the old logo — some in London, some in Sydney, for hours.
You could purge the edges — modern CDNs do that in seconds — but someone has to remember to, every time, and no purge can reach the copies already saved in users’ browsers.

callout.text: Long TTLs are what make a CDN fast — and what makes updates slow to appear.

changes: − Edges still serve the old one

steps.title: Give every version a new name
body: Put a fingerprint of the file’s contents in its name: logo.3f9a.png. A new logo gets a new name, so it can never be confused with the old one.
Now files can be cached for a year. The HTML (short TTL, or not cached) simply points at the latest names.

callout.text: Build tools such as Vite and webpack add these content hashes for you.

steps.title: Spikes hit the edge, not you
body: A launch goes viral and traffic jumps 20×. Almost all of it is answered by edges spread around the world; the origin barely notices.
The same spread-out capacity helps absorb floods of malicious traffic (DDoS attacks).

callout.text: A CDN is a cache, a global network and a shield for your origin, all at once.

steps.title: Case: never cache someone’s cart
body: A config change tells the CDN to cache every page for 5 minutes. Bob opens his cart; the edge stores it. Alice opens hers a second later — and the edge serves her Bob’s cart.
Pages that depend on who is asking must be marked Cache-Control: private (or no-store) so edges always pass them through to the origin.

callout.text: Caching personal data publicly is a classic, very public incident. Default to private; cache public content on purpose.

changes: + Cart and account pages: Cache-Control: private
~ Personal pages always go to the origin

steps.title: Origin shield: one more layer
body: A real CDN has hundreds of edges. When a new file goes viral, every edge misses once — hundreds of requests for the same file hit your origin at the same moment.
An origin shield is a mid-tier cache in front of the origin. Edges miss to the shield; only the shield ever asks the origin, so each file is fetched once.

callout.text: Most CDNs offer shielding as a setting. Pick a shield location close to your origin.

changes: + Origin shield between edges and origin
~ Origin sees one fetch per file

steps.title: Recap
body:
• Distance adds latency; edge servers move content close to users.
  • CDNs are pull-through caches: misses fill them from your origin.
  • Versioned file names let you cache for a year and still update instantly.
  • The edge absorbs spikes and shields the origin.
  • Never cache personal pages publicly; add an origin shield at scale.

callout.text: That wraps up Scaling. Next module: Data & Storage, starting with SQL vs NoSQL.

sql-nosql.title: SQL vs NoSQL
sql-nosql.summary: Tables, documents or plain keys — what each kind of database is good at, and what it gives up.

steps.title: Data in tables
body: Most apps start with a relational (SQL) database such as PostgreSQL or MySQL. Data lives in tables with a fixed set of columns — a schema.
Tables point at each other with keys, and a join combines them in one query: “every order with its customer’s name”.

callout.text: SQL databases have decades of tooling behind them. When unsure, they’re a very safe default.

steps.title: All or nothing: transactions
body: Moving $50 from Ana to Ben is two updates. If the server crashes between them, money disappears.
A transaction groups them: both happen, or neither does. Relational databases guarantee this (the ACID properties), which is why they hold payments, orders and inventory.

callout.text: ACID: Atomic (all or nothing), Consistent (rules hold), Isolated (no half-done views), Durable (committed means saved).

steps.title: Growing pains
body: Your product catalog lands in the same database. Shoes have sizes, laptops have CPUs, books have authors — so the products table sprouts hundreds of mostly-empty columns, and every new product type means another migration on a 400-million-row table. Some of those rewrite or lock the whole table for hours.
Meanwhile all writes still go through one database server.

callout.text: Rigid schemas and a single write server are the two classic pain points of relational databases at scale.

changes: + Product catalog in the SQL database

steps.title: Documents: each record its own shape
body: A document store (such as MongoDB) keeps each record as a self-contained document. A shoe and a laptop can have completely different fields, with no migration to run — though your code must now cope with every shape it has ever written.
Everything about one product lives together, so reading it is a single fetch, and documents spread naturally across many servers.

callout.text: Documents shine when you read and write whole objects at once — catalogs, profiles, content.

changes: ~ SQL database back to orders & users

steps.title: Key–value: just look it up
body: The simplest store of all: a key–value store (Redis, DynamoDB) maps a key to a value. No queries, no joins — get and set by key, in about a millisecond.
Because each key stands alone, the data splits across many nodes almost for free.

callout.text: Perfect for sessions, carts, feature flags and counters — anything you always fetch by one id.

steps.title: What NoSQL gives up
body: NoSQL stores scale out easily largely because they give things up: joins across records, multi-record transactions, and often strict consistency.

SQLNoSQL
Data shapeFixed tablesFlexible
JoinsYesIn your code
TransactionsAcross rowsUsually one record
Scaling writesHardBuilt in

These are defaults, not laws, and the lines keep blurring: PostgreSQL stores JSON documents, MongoDB and DynamoDB offer multi-record transactions, and distributed SQL databases (Spanner, CockroachDB) scale writes out while keeping joins and transactions — paying for it in latency and complexity.

callout.text: Picking NoSQL “for scale” you don’t have yet often means rebuilding joins and transactions by hand.

steps.title: Use each where it fits
body: Real systems mix them — polyglot persistence. Money and orders stay relational for transactions; the catalog lives in documents; sessions go to a key–value store.
Start with one database, and add another only when a kind of data clearly wants it.

callout.text: The question isn’t “SQL or NoSQL?” but “what does this data need: relations, flexibility, or raw lookup speed?”

steps.title: Case: “red running shoes”
body: Shoppers type free text into a search box. In SQL that becomes WHERE name LIKE '%red%' on millions of rows — slow, and it can’t rank results, handle typos or match “shoe” to “shoes”.
A search engine (Elasticsearch, OpenSearch) builds an inverted index: for every word, the list of documents containing it. It’s fed from the main database by a stream of changes.

callout.text: The search index is a copy, not the source of truth — it can always be rebuilt from the main database.

steps.title: More specialised stores
body: Search is one example of a store built for one access pattern. There are others, each much better than a general database at its job — and worse at everything else.
Reach for them when a workload clearly doesn’t fit, not by default: every extra store is more to run, secure, back up and keep in sync.

callout.text: Most systems run fine on one relational database for years. Add specialists one at a time, for a measured need.

steps.title: Recap
body:
• SQL: tables, joins and transactions — a safe default.
  • Documents: flexible, self-contained records that scale out.
  • Key–value: fastest and simplest, lookup by id only.
  • Choose per kind of data; many systems use several.
  • Specialists like search are copies fed from the source of truth.

callout.text: Next up: Indexes — why the same query can take 2 seconds or 2 milliseconds.

indexes.title: Indexes
indexes.summary: Why the same query can take two seconds or two milliseconds.

goals.text: What a full table scan costs
How a B-tree index finds a row
What indexes cost on every write
When an index can’t help — and how to check

steps.title: Finding one user takes two seconds
body: Logging in looks up a user by email. With 50 million users, it takes over two seconds — and it gets slower every day.
With nothing to guide it, the database does a full table scan: it reads every page of the table, checking each row. Watch the amber request crawl along.

callout.text: Scans grow with the table. Fine at a thousand rows; painful at fifty million.

steps.title: How a phone book does it
body: Nobody reads a phone book page by page. Because it’s sorted, you open the middle, see whether your name comes before or after, and throw away half the book. Repeat.
Halving 50 million entries takes only about 26 steps.

callout.text: An index is a sorted copy of one column, with a pointer back to each full row.

q.title: Sorted → binary search
lines: halve the range at every step

steps.title: Add an index
body: CREATE INDEX ON users (email) builds a B-tree: a small tree of sorted keys. The root says which branch covers your email, the branch says which page holds the row.
Three hops instead of fifty million rows: the lookup now takes about 2 ms.

callout.text: Primary keys get an index automatically. Columns you search, join or sort on usually need one too.

steps.title: Why B-trees stay shallow
body: Each tree node is one disk page holding hundreds of keys, so every level multiplies the reach by hundreds.
Three or four levels cover billions of rows — and the top levels are used so often they stay in memory.

callout.text: That’s why an indexed lookup costs about the same at a million rows as at a billion.

q.title: Fan-out per level
lines: = ~4 page reads to find any row

steps.title: Every index makes writes slower
body: When a user signs up, the row goes into the table and into every index on it, keeping each one sorted. Watch the writes (dark squares) land in both places.
Indexes also take disk and memory. Index what you query, not everything.

callout.text: A table with 6 indexes does 7 writes per insert. Unused indexes are pure cost.

steps.title: Composite indexes: order matters
body: An index can cover several columns, like (country, city). It’s sorted by country first, then by city within each country — like a phone book sorted by last name, then first name.
It speeds up queries on country, or country + city. A query on city alone can’t use it and falls back to a scan.

callout.text: Put the column you always filter on first. Indexes help from the left.

steps.title: Case: queries the index can’t help
body: Marketing asks for every Gmail user: WHERE email LIKE '%@gmail.com'. The index is sorted by the start of each email, and this pattern says nothing about the start — so it’s a full scan again.
The same happens with functions: WHERE LOWER(email) = … can’t use a plain index on email, because the index stores the original values.

callout.text: Fixes: an expression index on LOWER(email), a stored domain column with its own index, or a search engine for free-text matching.

steps.title: Case: the index nobody uses
body: Support wants every user in one country: WHERE country = 'US'. You add an index on country — and the database ignores it, because 40% of all rows match.

Following the index would mean hopping to a different table page for each of 20 million rows — slower than simply reading the table front to back. An index pays off when it is selective: when it narrows the search to a small fraction of the rows.

callout.text: If you only ever query a small slice — WHERE status = 'pending' — use a partial index that contains just those rows: tiny, fast and cheap to maintain.

changes: ~ 40% of rows match → full scan anyway

q.title: How many rows match?
lines: # an index helps when it rules out most rows

steps.title: Ask the database: EXPLAIN
body: You don’t have to guess. Prefix a query with EXPLAIN and the database shows its plan: which index it will use, and how many rows it expects to read.
“Index Scan” on a few rows is good news. “Seq Scan” on a big table is the red flag. EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query and reports real timings.

callout.text: Most databases also keep a slow-query log. Start there: it lists the queries actually costing you time.

q.title: EXPLAIN
lines: SELECT * FROM users WHERE email LIKE '%@g…'

steps.title: Covering indexes: skip the table
body: The login page only needs the user’s name and id. If the index stores those columns too, the database can answer from the index alone — it never visits the table pages.
This is a covering index. Watch lookups stop at the branches instead of reaching the table.

callout.text: In PostgreSQL: CREATE INDEX ON users (email) INCLUDE (id, name). It makes the index bigger, so cover only hot queries.

steps.title: Recap
body:
• Without an index, a lookup scans every row.
  • A B-tree index finds any row in a handful of page reads.
  • Every index adds work to every write — index what you query.
  • Composite indexes work from the leftmost column.
  • Leading wildcards, functions and low selectivity defeat indexes — check with EXPLAIN.

callout.text: Next up: Storage Engines — what the database actually does with a write, and why some are built for reads and others for writes.

storage-engines.title: Storage Engines
storage-engines.summary: What a database actually does with your write — and why some are built for reads and others for writes.

goals.text: How a B-tree engine reads and writes
LSM-trees: memtable, SSTables, Bloom filters, compaction
Choosing: B-tree or LSM, rows or columns

steps.title: Memory and disk
body: A database server has two places to keep data. Memory is fast — a change takes nanoseconds — but everything in it vanishes when the process stops. Disk survives a crash or a power cut, but a write that must be confirmed as truly on the device (an fsync) is thousands of times slower.

A storage engine is the part of the database that decides what goes where, and when. Every design is a different answer to one question: how do you get the speed of memory and the safety of disk at once?

callout.text: Tables are stored as fixed-size pages — typically 8 or 16 KB, each holding dozens of rows. The engine keeps recently used pages in memory and reads the rest from disk on demand.

steps.title: Fast and wrong: memory first, disk whenever
body: The simplest engine: change the page in memory, reply “saved”, and copy changed pages to disk every few seconds in the background. Writes are blazing fast.

Then the power fails. Everything changed since the last background copy is gone — including orders that customers were told had gone through. Worse, a page that was half-written when the power died is now garbage: a torn page.

callout.text: “Saved” has to mean “survives a crash”. That is the D in ACID — durability.

changes: + Reply “saved” as soon as memory is updated
− Power cut: the last few seconds of writes are lost

tags.text: power cut · 4 s of writes gone

steps.title: Write it down first: the write-ahead log
body: The obvious fix — push every changed page to disk before replying — is safe but painfully slow: a whole 8 KB page rewritten at a random position, to save one 100-byte row.

Instead, describe the change in a few bytes and append it to a log file, forcing that to disk before replying. This is the write-ahead log (WAL). Appending to the end of one file is the fastest thing a disk can do. The pages themselves are changed in memory and copied out later, at leisure.
<small>The speeds shown are for one ordinary SSD. Yours will differ; the ratios between the designs won’t.</small>

callout.text: After a crash the engine replays the log and rebuilds exactly the state it had promised — repairing any torn pages along the way. The log is the truth; the pages are a convenient summary of it.

changes: ~ “Saved” only once the log entry is on disk
~ Data pages are copied out later, in the background

steps.title: Case: how sure is “saved”?
body: Forcing the log to disk takes a fraction of a millisecond on an SSD, and by default it happens once per transaction. At thousands of commits a second, that one step becomes the limit.

Group commit helps for free: transactions that arrive in the same instant share a single fsync. Beyond that there is a dial. Most databases can sync on a timer instead — every 100 ms, or every second — multiplying throughput, and accepting that a crash loses the last moments of “saved” writes.

callout.text: Know where your dial is set. Redis in append-only mode syncs once a second by default; PostgreSQL with synchronous_commit = off and MySQL with innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit = 2 can both lose the last moments before a power cut.

changes: + Group commit: many transactions, one fsync
~ Optional: sync on a timer — faster, but a crash loses the last moments

card.title: The durability dial
lines: = group commit        same safety, shared fsync
fsync every 100 ms    fast · may lose 100 ms
! fsync never         fastest · may lose minutes

steps.title: The log can’t grow for ever
body: Left alone, the log would grow without limit, and recovering from a crash would mean replaying days of it. So every few minutes the engine takes a checkpoint: it copies all changed pages to the data file, notes “everything up to here is safely in the pages”, and throws the older log away.
Recovery then replays only the log written since the last checkpoint — seconds to a few minutes of work.

callout.text: A checkpoint is a burst of scattered page writes. Databases spread them out over time; when they can’t keep up, you see it as periodic latency spikes.

changes: + Checkpoint: copy changed pages out, trim the log
~ Crash recovery replays only the log since the checkpoint

steps.title: The classic engine: pages and B-trees, updated in place
body: What we just built is the design inside PostgreSQL, MySQL (InnoDB), SQL Server and Oracle. Data lives in fixed-size pages, found through B-trees (see Indexes) — in some engines the table itself is one. To change a row, the engine finds its page and modifies that page in place, with the log for safety.
It is excellent at reads. Any row is three or four page reads away — usually straight from memory — and neighbouring keys sit on neighbouring pages, so range scans are cheap.

callout.text: One copy of every row, at a known address. That is what makes reads predictable — and why every write has to go and find that address.

changes: ~ Writes: find the page, change it in place

steps.title: Case: a firehose of writes
body: Now the workload changes: sensor readings, chat messages, click events — 200,000 small writes a second, each for a different key. Every one lands on a different page. Memory fills with changed pages, and each must eventually be written back to its own spot on disk: a whole page, for a few bytes of change.
The log keeps up easily, because it is sequential. The scattered page writes don’t. Checkpoints fall behind, and write throughput is capped by how fast the disk can do random writes.

callout.text: This is write amplification: storing 100 bytes costs a log record plus an 8 KB page write. On a write-heavy workload the disk can end up writing tens of times more bytes than you actually stored.

changes: − Every page is dirty · checkpoints fall behind

steps.title: Never update in place: the LSM-tree
body: A different design drops the idea that each row has one home. A write goes to the log and into a sorted structure in memory, the memtable. That’s all — there is no page to find.

When the memtable fills up it is written to disk in one go as an immutable, sorted file — an SSTable — and a fresh memtable starts. Every disk write is sequential. This is the log-structured merge tree (LSM): the design behind Cassandra, HBase, ScyllaDB and RocksDB, the engine many other databases embed.

callout.text: An update is just a newer entry with the same key; a delete is a marker called a tombstone. Nothing already on disk is ever modified.

changes: + A full memtable is flushed as one sorted file

steps.title: Case: where is my key?
body: Reading is now the hard part. The newest value for a key might be in the memtable, or in any SSTable. Check them from newest to oldest: a key last written long ago — or one that doesn’t exist at all — costs a search of every file.

Two tricks rescue reads. Each SSTable carries a Bloom filter (see Caching) that answers “definitely not in this file” without touching the disk, and a small index of where each key range starts. A typical lookup then reads from just one file.

callout.text: B-trees pay at write time to keep reads simple. LSM-trees keep writes simple and pay at read time. Every storage engine sits somewhere on that line.

changes: − A lookup may have to check every SSTable
+ A Bloom filter and a small index per file
~ Most lookups read a single file

steps.title: Compaction: tidying up in the background
body: Files pile up, and the older ones are full of values that have since been overwritten or deleted. So a background process keeps merging SSTables: read a few sorted files, write one new sorted file that keeps only the newest value of each key, delete the inputs.

This is compaction. It limits how many files a read has to consider, and gives the space back. It is also the price of the design: every byte is rewritten several times over its life, and compaction competes with live traffic for the disk.

callout.text: If writes outrun compaction, files accumulate, reads slow down and the disk fills up. Watching the compaction backlog is the first rule of running an LSM database.

changes: + Compaction merges three files into one
− Overwritten values and tombstones are dropped
~ Fewer files to consider on every read

steps.title: B-tree or LSM?
body:
B-treeLSM-tree
WritesScattered page updatesSequential appends
ReadsA few pages, predictableSeveral files; filters help
SpacePages left part-emptyCompact, compresses well
BackgroundCheckpointsCompaction
Found inPostgreSQL, MySQLCassandra, RocksDB

Read-heavy, with range queries and transactions: a B-tree. Write-heavy, huge and mostly appended: an LSM-tree. Several newer SQL databases — CockroachDB, TiDB, MyRocks — put SQL on top of an LSM engine.

callout.text: You rarely choose a storage engine directly; you choose a database and inherit its engine. Knowing which one is underneath explains most of how it behaves under load.

steps.title: Case: rows or columns?
body: One more axis. Both engines so far keep each row together — ideal when you fetch or change whole records. But an analyst asks for SELECT SUM(price) FROM orders across two billion rows, and a row store has to read all 40 columns of every row to add up one of them.

A column store keeps each column in its own file. The query reads only price — a fortieth of the data — and because similar values sit side by side, it compresses several times over. That is how warehouses such as BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift and ClickHouse scan billions of rows in seconds.

callout.text: Row stores serve the app: many small reads and writes. Column stores serve analytics: a few enormous scans. It is why data gets copied from one to the other — see Batch & Stream Processing.

changes: + Analytics query: SUM(price) over 2 billion rows
− Row store: every column of every row is read

tags.text: column store · one file per column

steps.title: Recap
body:
• Memory is fast and forgetful; disk is durable and slow. A storage engine bridges the two.
  • The write-ahead log makes “saved” true: append, fsync, then reply.
  • How often you fsync is a durability dial — know where yours is set.
  • B-trees update pages in place: predictable reads, scattered writes.
  • LSM-trees only append: fast writes, paid for with compaction and harder reads.
  • Column stores serve analytics by reading only the columns a query needs.

callout.text: Next up: Replication — what to do when one database server can’t take all the reads, or might die.

replication.title: Replication
replication.summary: Keep copies of the database on several machines — for more reads and for survival.

goals.text: Leaders, followers and the replication log
Analytics replicas, backups and replication styles

steps.title: One database, doing everything
body: Every read and every write goes to a single database server. It’s 90% busy — and most of that is reads: product pages, profiles, feeds.
It’s also a single point of failure: if it dies, so does everything.

callout.text: Most apps read far more than they write — often 10 or 100 reads per write.

steps.title: Keep copies: leader and followers
body: Add two followers (replicas). The leader still takes every write, and streams each change to the followers through a replication log.
Each follower replays the changes and ends up with the same data.

callout.text: Also called primary/replica or master/slave. Built into PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB and most others.

steps.title: Send reads to the followers
body: Now the app sends reads to the followers and only writes to the leader. Read capacity doubles — two machines now do nothing but reads — and the leader cools down to 30%.
Need more reads? Add another follower.

callout.text: This works brilliantly for read-heavy apps. It doesn’t help write-heavy ones — every write still goes through one leader.

steps.title: Copies lag behind
body: Replication is usually asynchronous: the leader confirms a write right away and ships it to followers a moment later.
Alice renames herself, then reloads her profile. The read lands on a follower that hasn’t caught up — she sees her old name and thinks the save failed.

callout.text: Lag is normally milliseconds, but under load it can grow to seconds or minutes.

changes: − Follower still has the old one

steps.title: Read your own writes
body: A common fix: for a few seconds after someone writes, send their reads to the leader. Everyone else keeps using followers.
The other option is synchronous replication: the leader waits for a follower to confirm before saying “saved”. No lag — but slower writes, and they stall if that follower is down.

callout.text: For data you can’t afford to lose, a common setup is one synchronous follower (for safety) and the rest asynchronous (for speed). Many systems stay fully asynchronous and accept losing the last moments of writes in a crash.

steps.title: The leader dies
body: The leader crashes. Reads keep working — the followers still have the data — but every write now fails. Nobody can sign up, post or pay.

callout.text: Followers protect your reads. Writes need a new leader.

steps.title: Failover: promote a follower
body: Failover: the most up-to-date follower is promoted to leader, the app points its writes there, and the other follower replicates from it. A fresh follower is added to restore the spare.
Writes resume within seconds to a minute. Any writes the old leader hadn’t shipped yet may be lost — another reason to keep one follower synchronous.

The hard part is being sure the leader is dead. If it was only slow or cut off, you now have two leaders both accepting writes — split brain. Doing this safely takes a majority vote: see Consensus & Leader Election.

callout.text: Same idea as the standby load balancer: a spare that takes over. Managed databases automate it.

steps.title: Case: the 20-minute report
body: The finance team runs a monthly report — a 20-minute query that scans years of orders. They point it at a follower, and that follower, which also serves the app’s reads, grinds to a halt and falls minutes behind.
Fix: a dedicated analytics replica that the app never reads from. Heavy queries can be as slow as they like there.

callout.text: At larger scale, copy data into a separate analytics warehouse (BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift) built for huge scans.

changes: + Analytics replica, outside the app’s read pool
~ Reports no longer slow the app

steps.title: Case: the migration with no WHERE
body: A deploy runs a migration with a missing WHERE: UPDATE users SET email = NULL. The leader obeys — and replication faithfully copies the mistake to every follower within a second.

Replicas protect you from a machine failing, not from a bad write. For that you need backups: a nightly snapshot plus the archived write log, which together can rebuild the database as it was at any chosen moment — point-in-time recovery.

callout.text: A backup you have never restored is a hope, not a backup. Rehearse restores, and know how long one takes.

changes: ~ Restore to 14:02, a minute before the mistake

steps.title: Three ways to replicate
body: Everything so far was single-leader: one writer, many readers. It’s simple and it’s what most SQL databases do.

Multi-leader puts a leader in each region so writes stay local — at the cost of conflicts when two regions edit the same row. Leaderless systems (Cassandra, Riak, ScyllaDB — the “Dynamo-style” databases) write to several copies at once and read from several — the quorums in the CAP lesson.

callout.text: Prefer single-leader until you have a concrete reason (global writes, extreme availability) to take on conflict handling.

card.title: Replication styles
lines: leaderless     write N, read R · quorums

steps.title: Recap
body:
• A leader takes writes and streams them to followers.
  • Followers scale reads and survive losing a machine.
  • Async replicas lag: route a user’s reads to the leader right after they write.
  • When the leader dies, fail over to a follower.
  • Keep heavy analytics on its own replica.
  • Replicas are not backups: keep snapshots and rehearse restoring them.

callout.text: Next up: Sharding — for when even the leader can’t keep up with the writes.

sharding.title: Sharding
sharding.summary: When the data or the writes outgrow one machine, split them across many.

goals.text: Why replicas don’t help with writes
Why adding a shard is painful

steps.title: Too big for one machine
body: The users database has grown to 20 TB and takes 40,000 writes a second. Followers would help with reads — but every write still has to go through one leader, and all the data has to fit on its disks.
You’re already on the biggest machine, and every backup, restore or new replica now takes the best part of a day to copy.

callout.text: Replication copies all the data everywhere. To scale writes and storage, the data itself has to be split.

steps.title: Split the data: sharding
body: Sharding splits one big database into several smaller ones — shards — each holding part of the data and taking part of the writes.
A shard key decides where each row lives. Here: by user id range. The app (or a router) looks up the range and sends each query to the right shard.

callout.text: Each shard is usually replicated too: shards scale writes, followers within a shard scale reads and survive failures.

steps.title: Ranges create hot spots
body: User ids grow over time, so every new signup lands in the last range. New users are also the most active — and shard D ends up with most of the writes while A sits nearly idle.
The same happens with dates or alphabetical names: data that arrives in order piles onto one shard.
Range-partitioned databases (Bigtable, HBase, CockroachDB) soften this by splitting a busy range in two automatically — but writes that always land at the “end” simply follow the last range.

callout.text: A shard key must spread both the data and the traffic.

steps.title: Hash the key
body: Instead of ranges, run the key through a hash function and take the remainder: shard = hash(user_id) % 4.
Consecutive ids scatter to unrelated shards, so new users — and their traffic — spread evenly.

callout.text: Hashing loses range queries (“all users with ids 1–1000” now touches every shard). Usually a fine trade.

steps.title: Case: the celebrity
body: Hashing spreads keys evenly, not traffic. A pop star with 50 million followers lives on shard C like anyone else — and every view of their profile, every like on their posts, lands there too.
Shard C is melting while A, B and D are fine. This is a hot key, sometimes called the celebrity problem.

callout.text: No shard key fixes a single key that is more popular than one machine can handle.

changes: + One very popular user on shard C

steps.title: Cache it, or split it
body: For a key that is read hot, put it in a cache (or many cache replicas) in front of the shard — most profile views never reach it.
For a key that is write hot, like the pop star’s like counter, split it: write to likes:42#0 … likes:42#7 at random, spread across shards, and add them up when reading.

callout.text: Systems that face this daily (social networks, ticketing) treat their top keys specially — detected automatically, handled on purpose.

steps.title: Queries that span every shard
body: Looking up one user is fast: hash the id, ask one shard. But “top 10 users by followers” isn’t keyed by user — the app must ask every shard and merge the answers.
These scatter–gather queries are as slow as the slowest shard, and joins across shards are hard.

callout.text: Pick a shard key that matches your most important queries — ideally they only ever touch one shard.

card.title: Scatter–gather
lines: ask all 4 shards for their top 10
! as slow as the slowest shard

steps.title: Adding a shard moves almost everything
body: Shards fill up, so you add a fifth. But hash % 4 becomes hash % 5 — and for about 80% of users the remainder changes.
Terabytes have to move between shards while the system keeps serving traffic.

callout.text: With hash % N, changing N reshuffles nearly every key. The next lesson fixes exactly this.

steps.title: Recap
body:
• Sharding splits data and writes across machines.
  • The shard key decides where rows live — it must spread load evenly.
  • Ranges make hot spots; hashes spread load but scatter range queries.
  • A single hot key needs caching or splitting.
  • Queries off the shard key hit every shard; resharding with % N moves most data.

callout.text: Next up: Consistent Hashing — add or remove a shard and move only a fraction of the keys.

consistent-hashing.title: Consistent Hashing
consistent-hashing.summary: Add or remove servers and move only a sliver of the data.

goals.text: Keys belong to the next server clockwise
Adding or removing a server moves one arc
Virtual nodes even out the load
Replicas on the ring, and cache clusters

steps.title: hash % N breaks when N changes
body: Last lesson ended badly: with shard = hash(key) % N, going from 4 to 5 shards changes the answer for about 80% of keys. Nearly all the data moves.
We want a scheme where adding a server only moves the keys that server should take over — roughly 1/N of them.

callout.text: The trick is to stop tying placement to N at all.

steps.title: Bend the hash space into a ring
body: Hash values run from 0 to 2³². Join the ends and you get a ring.
Now hash each server’s name too, and place it on the ring at that point. The servers glide to wherever their hashes put them — not evenly spaced, just wherever the hash lands.

callout.text: Nothing here depends on how many servers there are. That’s the whole point.

steps.title: Each key goes clockwise
body: Hash each key onto the ring too. A key belongs to the first server clockwise from it. The coloured arcs show which server owns which stretch; each dot is a key, coloured by its owner.
Watch a lookup travel clockwise from a key to its server.

callout.text: To find a key’s server: hash the key, walk clockwise, stop at the first server. Clients do this with a sorted list and a binary search.

changes: ~ Each key owned by the next server clockwise

steps.title: Adding a server moves one arc
body: Server E joins at its hash position, between C and B. It takes over only the keys in the arc just counter-clockwise of it — the ones that used to walk past it to C.
Every other key stays exactly where it was. The pulsing keys are the only ones that move.

callout.text: Adding the 5th server moves about 1/5 of the keys — the minimum possible.

steps.title: Removing a server moves one arc too
body: Back to four servers — and now C dies. Its keys simply continue clockwise to the next server, D. Nobody else is affected.
Compare that with % N, where losing one server would reshuffle almost everything.

callout.text: Amazon’s Dynamo, Cassandra and many caches and CDNs place data this way. Close cousins — rendezvous and jump hashing — get the same result without a ring.

steps.title: Random positions, uneven arcs
body: Servers land wherever their hash puts them, so arcs are uneven. With C gone, D now owns a huge stretch of the ring — and gets far more keys and traffic than A or B.
With only a few servers, luck alone can leave one doing twice the work of another.

callout.text: Uneven arcs mean uneven load — exactly the hot spot sharding was meant to avoid.

steps.title: Virtual nodes even it out
body: Give each server several positions on the ring — virtual nodes (the diamonds) — by hashing A#1, A#2, … Each server now owns many small arcs instead of one big one.
Shares even out, and when a server leaves, its keys spread across all the others instead of dumping on one neighbour.

callout.text: Real systems use anywhere from 16 to a few hundred virtual nodes per server. Stronger servers can get more of them.

steps.title: Copies on the next servers clockwise
body: One copy per key isn’t enough — a dead server would lose its data. So each key is stored on the first three distinct servers clockwise: its owner plus the next two.
Follow the key at 160°: copy 1 on A, copy 2 on B, copy 3 on C. If A dies, B and C still have it, and the next server along takes over A’s share.

callout.text: Dynamo calls this the preference list. With virtual nodes, skip positions owned by a server you already picked.

steps.title: Case: growing a cache cluster
body: A fleet of Memcached servers sits in front of a database, and clients pick a server with hash(key) % N. Adding a fifth server remaps ~80% of keys — they all miss at once, and the database is flattened by the stampede.
With consistent hashing, adding the fifth server moves only ~20% of keys. The cache stays mostly warm and the database barely notices.

callout.text: This is where consistent hashing started: spreading web caches across machines that come and go.

steps.title: Recap
body:
• Put servers and keys on a hash ring; a key belongs to the next server clockwise.
  • Adding or removing a server moves only one arc — about 1/N of keys.
  • Virtual nodes even out shares and spread the load when servers leave.
  • Store each key on the next N servers clockwise for redundancy.

callout.text: Next up: Unique IDs at Scale — giving every row a name once there is no single database to count for you.

unique-ids.title: Unique IDs at Scale
unique-ids.summary: Giving every row a name nobody else will ever use — without one counter everyone has to queue for.

goals.text: Why database counters break under sharding
UUIDs — and what random keys do to an index
Time-ordered ids: UUID v7 and Snowflake
Clocks that step back, and what ids leak

steps.title: Every row needs a name
body: Orders, users, payments: every row needs an identifier that is unique — for ever. Other tables point at it, URLs contain it, support staff read it out over the phone.
With one database this is free. An AUTO_INCREMENT (or SERIAL) column hands out 1001, 1002, 1003… and the database guarantees no number is ever used twice.

callout.text: A counter gives you more than uniqueness: the ids are small, and sorting by id sorts by creation time. Watch which of those gifts each alternative keeps.

steps.title: Two shards, two counters
body: The orders table gets sharded (see Sharding). Each shard is its own database with its own counter — and both of them have just handed out 1004.
Two different orders now share an id. A link to /orders/1004, a cache entry, a refund: each could mean either one. And the day you merge or re-split shards, the rows collide.

callout.text: Uniqueness has to hold across the whole system, not just inside one machine.

changes: + Shard B, with its own counter

steps.title: Way 1 — one counter for everyone
body: Move the counter out of the shards into a small service whose only job is to hand out the next number: a ticket server. Before each insert, an app server asks it for an id.
Uniqueness is back, and ids still sort by time. But every insert now costs an extra round trip — and if the ticket server is down, nobody can create anything.

callout.text: Flickr ran two ticket servers for years — one handing out odd numbers, the other even — so that either could fail without stopping the site.

changes: ~ Every insert asks it for an id first
− A new single point of failure

steps.title: Hand out blocks, not single numbers
body: Ask less often. Each app server reserves a whole block — say 1,000 ids — in one call and hands them out from memory. That’s one round trip per thousand inserts, and the app keeps working for a while if the ticket server is down.
The price: ids no longer follow creation time across servers (Server 2’s 2001 may be older than Server 1’s 1500), and a server that crashes takes the rest of its block with it, leaving gaps.

callout.text: Gaps are harmless. Never promise that ids are gap-free or strictly ordered — invoice numbers that legally must be gapless are a separate, deliberate counter.

steps.title: Way 2 — pick a number nobody else will
body: Or drop the coordination altogether. A UUID (version 4) is 122 random bits. Any server, phone or script can make one, with nobody to ask.
Can two collide? In principle. In practice you would have to generate a billion every second for about 86 years to reach a 50% chance of a single repeat.
