callout.text: The cost is size: 128 bits, twice a normal id — and that id is copied into every index and every table that points at the row.

steps.title: Case: random ids and the index
body: The primary key lives in a B-tree, sorted by id (see Indexes). Counter ids always land on the last page, which stays in memory. Random ids land on a random page, every time.

Once the index is bigger than memory, most inserts must first fetch a cold page from disk, and pages split all over the tree. Insert throughput can drop several-fold, and the index ends up bloated with half-empty pages.

callout.text: It bites hardest where the table itself is stored in primary-key order — MySQL’s InnoDB, SQL Server — but every B-tree feels it.

changes: + Inside one shard: the primary-key index

tags.text: primary-key index · pages sorted by id →

card.title: Where does the next row go?
lines: counter id   → always the last page
! random id  → any page, every time

steps.title: Put the time in front
body: Keep the randomness, but lead with a timestamp. UUID v7 — and its cousin, ULID — starts with 48 bits of milliseconds, followed by random bits.
New ids are always larger than old ones, so inserts return to the right-hand edge of the index. They still need no coordination, and “sort by id” means “sort by creation time” again.

callout.text: If you want UUIDs as primary keys, use version 7. Keep version 4 for tokens that must be impossible to guess.

changes: ~ Inserts append to the last page again

tags.text: primary-key index · pages sorted by id →

steps.title: Way 3 — Snowflake ids
body: Twitter needed ids that fit in 64 bits, sort by time, and could be minted tens of thousands of times a second with no central counter. Its answer, Snowflake, packs three fields into one number.

A millisecond timestamp, the machine id of the generator, and a sequence that counts up within the millisecond. Two machines can never collide, because their machine ids differ; one machine never repeats, because of the sequence.

callout.text: Each machine can mint 4,096 ids per millisecond. Discord, Instagram and many others use the same idea with slightly different bit splits.

changes: + Every server gets a machine id at startup

steps.title: Case: the clock steps back
body: Snowflake ids are unique only if a machine’s clock never repeats a millisecond. But clocks get corrected: time sync notices Server 1 is two seconds fast and sets it back. For two seconds it would stamp ids with times it has already used — duplicates.
The guard is simple. Remember the last timestamp you issued; if the clock now reads earlier, wait (or refuse to issue ids) until time has caught up.

callout.text: The other way to break it: two machines with the same machine id. Assign them from one place — a config service, or bits of something already unique — never by hand.

changes: + Generator waits until the clock passes its last stamp
~ No duplicates — that server pauses inserts for 2 s

steps.title: Case: what an id gives away
body: Ids end up in URLs, and people read them. A competitor places an order on Monday (#1004) and another on Tuesday (#1250) — and now knows you take about 246 orders a day.
Sequential ids are also easy to walk: change /invoices/1004 to /invoices/1005 and see what comes back. Time-based ids reveal exactly when each thing was created.

callout.text: Two defences, and you need the second one regardless: show a separate random public id, and check authorization on every request (see Authorization). An unguessable id is not access control.

changes: + A competitor reading ids out of URLs
~ Public ids → random; internal keys stay ordered

steps.title: Which id for which job
body:
SizeTime-sortedNeeds
DB counter64 bitsYesOne database
Ticket blocks64 bitsRoughlyA ticket service
UUID v4128 bitsNoNothing
UUID v7128 bitsYesA clock
Snowflake64 bitsYesMachine ids + clock
One database? Use its counter. Many writers and nothing shared? UUID v7. Compact numeric ids at very high volume? Snowflake.

callout.text: There is no best id — only the properties your system needs: size, ordering, independence and secrecy.

steps.title: Recap
body:
• A per-database counter stops being unique the moment you shard.
  • A ticket server restores it; handing out blocks removes the round trip per insert.
  • UUID v4 needs nobody, but scatters inserts across the index; UUID v7 puts time first to fix that.
  • Snowflake: time + machine id + sequence in 64 bits — guard against clocks stepping back.
  • Ids leak volume and timing. Never treat them as access control.

callout.text: Next up: CAP & Consistency — what copies of your data should do when the network between them breaks.

cap.title: CAP & Consistency
cap.summary: When the network splits, copies of your data must choose between being right and being reachable.

steps.title: Copies in two regions
body: A ticket site keeps a copy of its data in Europe and in the US, so each region’s users get fast answers. Every write is replicated to the other side.
One concert has 1 seat left, and both copies agree.

callout.text: Replicating across regions buys speed and survival — and opens the question this lesson is about.

steps.title: The network splits
body: An undersea cable is cut. Both regions are healthy and their users can still reach them — but the regions can’t talk to each other. This is a network partition.
Now a US user wants to buy the last seat. The US copy can’t check with Europe. What should it do?

callout.text: Partitions aren’t rare: cables, routers, misconfigurations and overloaded links all cause them.

steps.title: Option 1: stay consistent
body: Refuse what can’t be confirmed. Europe holds the primary copy, so it keeps serving; the US side rejects writes — and reads that might be stale — until the link is back.
Nobody ever sees wrong data. But US users get errors for as long as the partition lasts.

callout.text: Choose consistency where wrong answers cost money: payments, bank balances, inventory, ticket sales.

steps.title: Option 2: stay available
body: Answer with what you have. Both sides keep accepting writes. Ana in Paris buys the last seat. Ben in Boston buys the last seat.
Everyone gets an answer — and the two copies now disagree. When the link returns, there are two sales of one seat.

callout.text: Choose availability where a brief disagreement is fine: likes, view counts, shopping carts, social feeds.

steps.title: Healing: eventual consistency
body: The cable is repaired and the copies exchange what they missed. Left alone they will converge — eventual consistency — but someone has to decide what to do with the conflict.
Options: last write wins (simple, silently drops one sale), or let the app merge (keep both, refund one, apologise).

callout.text: “Last write wins” is the default in many databases. It loses data quietly — make sure that’s acceptable.

steps.title: Case: “last” by whose clock?
body: Last write wins needs to know which write was last — and each server stamps writes with its own clock. Clocks drift. Here the US server’s clock runs 3 seconds fast.

A customer saves a delivery address through the US copy, then corrects it two seconds later through the EU copy. The correction is newer, but its timestamp is smaller — so when the copies sync, last write wins keeps the old address and silently throws the fix away.

callout.text: Never order events across machines by wall-clock time. Use version numbers or logical clocks (Lamport timestamps, version vectors) that count events instead of reading the time — or keep both versions and let the app merge.

changes: − The newer write carries the older timestamp
− Last write wins keeps the wrong address

steps.title: What CAP actually says
body: The CAP theorem: when a network Partition happens, a replicated system must give up either Consistency (every read sees the latest write, as if there were only one copy) or Availability (every request to a working server gets an answer).
You don’t “pick two of three” — partitions will happen, so the real choice is what to do when they do.
CAP’s “consistency” is what database people call linearizability. It is not the C in ACID, which is about a transaction keeping your data’s rules intact.

callout.text: PACELC adds the everyday half: even without a partition, keeping copies in sync costs latency. Consistency is never free.

card.title: During a partition, choose
lines: # without a partition: latency vs consistency

steps.title: Quorums: tune the trade-off
body: Many databases let you choose per request. With N = 3 copies, a write waits for W copies to confirm and a read asks R copies, using the newest answer.
If W + R > N, every read overlaps at least one copy that saw the latest write — here W = 2 and R = 2, so a read always reaches a v2 even though one copy is stale.

callout.text: W = 1, R = 1: fast and available, possibly stale. W = 3: every copy must answer — consistent but fragile. Cassandra, Riak and ScyllaDB expose these knobs per request; DynamoDB offers the simpler choice of eventual or strongly consistent reads.

steps.title: Case: a payment and a like
body: One app, two very different writes. A like can be confirmed by one copy and spread later (W = 1, R = 1): fast, always available, and nobody minds if a count is briefly off.

Recording a payment (the big square) uses a majority for both the write and every read (W = 2, R = 2): slower, and it fails if two copies can’t be reached — rather than risk anyone reading a stale “unpaid”.

callout.text: You don’t pick consistency once for the whole system. Pick it per operation, by asking what a wrong answer would cost.

steps.title: Consistency is a spectrum
body: “Consistent” isn’t yes or no. Between the strongest (linearizable: everyone sees the latest write) and eventual sit useful promises: read-your-writes (you always see your own changes), monotonic reads (time never goes backwards for you), and causal consistency (replies never appear before the message they answer).
Weaker promises are cheaper and more available. Pick the weakest one your users won’t notice.

callout.text: Many “eventual” systems offer read-your-writes per session — enough for most apps.

card.title: Strongest → weakest
lines: monotonic      never go back in time

steps.title: Recap
body:
• A partition splits copies that can each still serve users.
  • During one, choose consistency (refuse) or availability (answer, maybe stale).
  • Available systems are eventually consistent and must resolve conflicts — without trusting wall clocks.
  • Quorums (W + R > N) tune the trade-off per request.
  • Pick the weakest consistency each operation can tolerate.

callout.text: Next up: Consensus & Leader Election — how a group of servers agrees on one truth, even when some of them can’t be reached.

consensus.title: Consensus & Leader Election
consensus.summary: How a group of servers agrees on one leader and one history — even when some of them can’t be reached.

goals.text: Why naive failover causes split brain
Majority quorums — and why they overlap
When a write counts as committed
How many nodes a cluster needs

steps.title: One leader, two followers
body: From Replication: one leader takes every write and copies it to its followers. If the leader dies, a follower is promoted and carries on.
That sentence hides one of the hardest questions in distributed systems: who decides the leader is dead — and what happens if they’re wrong?

callout.text: From the outside, a crashed server, a slow server and a server behind a broken cable all look exactly the same: silence.

steps.title: Two leaders at once
body: A network fault cuts A off from B and C. A is alive and still serving App Server 1 — but B hears nothing, assumes the leader is dead, and promotes itself.
Now two leaders accept writes. Through A, seat 7 is sold to Ana; through B, the same seat is sold to Ben. Two histories that can never be merged cleanly: split brain.

callout.text: A timeout can tell you a server is unreachable. It can never tell you the server is dead.

changes: − Network between A and the others is cut

steps.title: The rule: nothing counts without a majority
body: The fix is one rule. A leader is only elected — and a write only confirmed — when more than half of all nodes agree. With three nodes, that’s two.

Cut off, A can reach only itself: 1 of 3. It can’t confirm anything, so App Server 1’s writes wait and time out. B and C are 2 of 3: they may elect a leader and carry on. Any two majorities share at least one node, so two leaders can never both win.

callout.text: This is CAP in practice: the minority side gives up availability so that the data stays consistent.

card.title: Majority (quorum)
lines: # so only one side can ever decide

steps.title: How a leader gets elected
body: This is the Raft algorithm. A leader sends regular heartbeats. Every follower runs a timer of random length; if it runs out with no heartbeat, that follower becomes a candidate.

B’s timer fires first. It starts term 2, votes for itself and asks the others. A node gives one vote per term, and only to a candidate whose log is at least as complete as its own. C says yes — 2 of 3 — so B leads term 2.

callout.text: Random timers mean two nodes rarely stand at once. If the vote does split, nobody wins, the timers restart, and the next term settles it — usually within a second.

changes: + B: no heartbeat → candidate for term 2
~ B wins 2 of 3 and starts sending heartbeats

card.title: Election · term 2
lines: # one vote per node per term

steps.title: A write is committed by a majority
body: Writes follow the same rule. App Server 2 sends seat 7 → Ben to the leader. B appends it to its log and sends it to the followers.
As soon as a majority has stored the entry — B and C — it is committed. Only then does B apply it and answer “saved”. A committed entry survives any failure that leaves a majority standing.

callout.text: Every node applies the same log entries in the same order, so every node ends up in the same state. That’s a replicated state machine — the idea underneath all of this.

changes: + B appends entry 4 to its log

steps.title: The old leader steps down
body: The network heals. A — still believing it leads term 1 — receives a heartbeat from B stamped term 2. A higher term always wins: A becomes a follower at once.

A’s log holds one entry that never reached a majority: Ana’s booking, which App Server 1 was never told had succeeded. A discards it and copies B’s log instead. All three nodes are identical again, and nothing that was confirmed has been lost.

callout.text: Terms are a logical clock. Nobody compares wall-clock times — only “whose term number is higher?”

changes: ~ A copies the log from B · apps follow the leader

steps.title: How many nodes?
body: A cluster of N nodes needs ⌊N/2⌋ + 1 votes, so it keeps working with ⌊(N − 1)/2⌋ of them down. Three nodes survive one failure; five survive two.

A fourth node is a trap: the majority becomes 3, so you still survive only one failure — with one more machine that can fail. Use odd sizes, and put each node in a different zone so one outage can’t take a majority with it.

callout.text: Three or five is typical. Every write waits for more acknowledgements as the cluster grows, so bigger clusters get slower, not safer.

steps.title: Case: the leader that paused
body: Leader B freezes for twenty seconds — a long garbage-collection pause, or its virtual machine being moved. A and C hear no heartbeats, elect C for term 3, and move on.

Then B wakes up. As far as it can tell no time has passed, and it is still the leader. Before the next message corrects it, it finishes what it was doing: writing a file to shared storage — straight over the new leader’s work.

callout.text: A node cannot know it was paused. “I checked that I was the leader a moment ago” is never proof that you still are.

changes: + A and C elect C · term 3
− B wakes up and writes as if it still led

steps.title: Fencing tokens
body: The fix doesn’t depend on B noticing anything. Every request a leader sends carries its term number as a fencing token, and the storage remembers the highest token it has seen.
C has already written with token 3. When B’s write arrives carrying token 2, the storage refuses it. The stale leader is fenced off by the resource itself.

callout.text: The same goes for distributed locks: the lock service must hand out an increasing number with each lock, and the protected resource must check it. A lock that only says “it’s yours” is not safe.

changes: + Every write carries the leader’s term
+ Storage rejects tokens older than the newest it has seen

steps.title: What consensus costs
body: Every write waits for a round trip to a majority. Inside one data center that’s a millisecond or two; with nodes in different regions it’s 50–150 ms on every write.
All writes pass through one leader, so throughput is capped by a single machine. And when no majority can be reached, the cluster accepts no writes at all — on purpose.

callout.text: Consensus buys correctness with latency and availability. Spend it on the small, critical decisions — not on every like and page view.

changes: ~ An election pauses writes for about a second

steps.title: You use it far more than you write it
body: Almost nobody implements Raft or Paxos themselves. You run a small consensus cluster — etcd, ZooKeeper or Consul — and keep only the critical facts in it: who the leader is, what the configuration says, who holds which lock.

Everything else leans on it. Kubernetes keeps all its cluster state in etcd. Kafka elects its controllers with Raft. Databases such as CockroachDB, Spanner and MongoDB run consensus inside every shard or replica set to decide failover.

callout.text: When the Replication lesson said “promote the most up-to-date follower”, this is the machinery that makes it safe.

changes: + Three systems that depend on the cluster

steps.title: Recap
body:
• A timeout can’t tell dead from unreachable — naive failover risks split brain.
  • Majority rule: elections and writes need more than half the nodes, and two majorities always overlap.
  • Terms order the leaders: a higher term wins and a stale leader steps down.
  • A write is committed once a majority has logged it — never before.
  • Run 3 or 5 nodes across zones, and use fencing tokens for anything outside the log.

callout.text: Next up: Transactions & Isolation — keeping one database correct when many requests change it at once.

transactions.title: Transactions & Isolation
transactions.summary: Two people, one seat, the same millisecond. How databases keep concurrent changes correct.

goals.text: Deadlocks and constraints as a safety net
Short transactions with holds that expire

steps.title: One seat left
body: Ana and Ben both want the last seat at a concert. Their requests land on different app servers, which share one database.
The booking code looks reasonable: read how many seats are left, and if there’s one, write the booking.

callout.text: Each request on its own is correct. The trouble only appears when two run at the same time.

card.title: Book a seat
lines: n = SELECT left FROM seats WHERE id = 7
# n − 1 is worked out in the app

steps.title: Both of them get it
body: Both servers read “1 seat left” before either has written. Both decide the seat is free, both write, and both send a confirmation.
One seat, two tickets. This is a race condition — here a lost update: Ben’s write silently overwrote Ana’s.

callout.text: Races are rare in testing and common in production — exactly when it’s busiest, like the moment tickets go on sale.

steps.title: A transaction alone doesn’t stop it
body: Wrap it in BEGIN … COMMIT and the booking becomes all-or-nothing — but it can still be sold twice. Under the default isolation level of most databases (read committed), each read simply sees the latest committed value: 1.
Isolation is the part of a transaction that says what concurrent transactions can see of each other. The default is deliberately weak, for speed.

callout.text: ACID’s “I” is a dial, not a switch. Know which level your database uses by default (PostgreSQL and SQL Server: read committed; MySQL: repeatable read).

steps.title: Lock the row while you decide
body: Read with SELECT … FOR UPDATE. Ana’s transaction locks row 7; when Ben’s tries to read it, the database makes him wait until Ana commits (watch his request hold at the database).
Then Ben reads the new value — 0 — and gets a polite “sold out”.

callout.text: Locks are held until COMMIT, so keep these transactions short: never wait for a user, a payment API or anything slow while holding one.

changes: + Ben waits ~40 ms for Ana’s lock

steps.title: Or do it in one statement
body: Often you don’t need to read first at all. Let the database check and change in one atomic step:
UPDATE seats SET left = left − 1 WHERE id = 7 AND left > 0 — then look at how many rows it changed. 1 means you got the seat; 0 means it was gone.

callout.text: Counters, stock levels and balances are usually safest as a single conditional UPDATE. No gap between check and change, no lock held across round trips.

changes: ~ Check and change in one UPDATE
~ Ben’s update changes 0 rows → sold out

steps.title: Optimistic: check a version number
body: Locks are pessimistic: they assume a conflict and make others wait. Optimistic concurrency assumes conflicts are rare: read the row with its version, then write … WHERE id = 7 AND version = 8, bumping it to 9.
If someone got there first, the version no longer matches, the write changes 0 rows, and you reload and try again. Nobody waits.

callout.text: Ideal when users edit things for a while — a document, a profile, a cart. Holding a lock for minutes would block everyone.

changes: ~ Ben’s write rejected (version changed) → retries → sold out

steps.title: Isolation levels
body: Databases offer several isolation levels. Stronger ones prevent more anomalies, but make transactions wait or abort more often.

PreventsCost
Read committedDirty readsLowest
Snapshot / repeatable read+ changing reads; lost updates in some databases1Some aborts
SerializableEverything: as if one at a timeMost aborts — retry
<small><sup>1</sup> PostgreSQL aborts the second writer; MySQL’s repeatable read lets the lost update through. Same name, different guarantees — check your database’s documentation.</small>

callout.text: With serializable, the database may abort a transaction rather than allow an anomaly. Your code must catch that and retry.

steps.title: Case: locking a row that doesn’t exist yet
body: A new booking flow drops the seat counter and checks the bookings table instead: “is there a booking for seat 7? No — insert one.” Both transactions even use FOR UPDATE…

…but there is no row to lock yet. Both see nothing, both insert, and seat 7 is booked twice. A row that appears between your check and your write is a phantom; deciding on what you read and then writing something else is called write skew.

callout.text: Fixes: serializable isolation, locking an existing parent row (the seat itself), or a unique constraint — see the next steps.

changes: − FOR UPDATE finds no row to lock

steps.title: Case: the deadlock
body: Locks bring their own trap. Ana transfers money from account A to B: she locks A, then asks for B. At the same instant Ben transfers from B to A: he locks B, then asks for A.
Each waits for the other, forever. The database detects the cycle — immediately in some engines, after about a second in others — and aborts one transaction (Ben’s), which must retry.

callout.text: Prevent it by always taking locks in the same order — for example, lowest account id first. Then a cycle can’t form.

changes: + Two transfers lock A and B in opposite orders

tags.text: Ana holds A · waits for B
Ben holds B · waits for A

card.title: A wait cycle
lines: Ana: lock A … waiting for B
Ben: lock B … waiting for A
= fix: always lock lowest id first

steps.title: Constraints: the last line of defence
body: Code changes, and someone will eventually write a booking path that forgets the lock. So let the database enforce the rule itself: a unique constraint on (concert, seat) in the bookings table.
Now a second booking for seat 7 is rejected with a duplicate-key error, whatever the application code does.

callout.text: Encode invariants as constraints — unique, foreign key, check (balance ≥ 0). They hold even when the code has bugs.

steps.title: Case: a lock held during a payment
body: To be safe, someone moves the card payment inside the booking transaction: lock seat 7, call the payment provider, then commit. The provider takes 3 seconds.
For those 3 seconds the seat stays locked, and every other buyer of it waits — each holding a database connection. On sale day the connection pool runs dry and the whole site stalls.

callout.text: Never wait on anything slow — a user, a payment API, an email — while holding a database lock or an open transaction.

changes: ~ Seat 7 locked for 3 s per attempt

steps.title: Reserve, pay, then confirm
body: Split it into short steps. Transaction 1 marks seat 7 as held for Ana until 12:10 and commits at once. Then she pays — outside any transaction. Transaction 2 marks the seat sold.
If she never pays, a cleanup job releases holds that have expired. Ben is told immediately that the seat is taken — no waiting, no locks held for seconds.

callout.text: This is the “seat held for 10 minutes” timer on every ticket and airline site. A reservation with an expiry replaces a long lock.

steps.title: Recap
body:
• Read-then-write under concurrency causes races and lost updates.
  • Fix with row locks, a single atomic UPDATE, or version checks.
  • Isolation levels trade correctness for waiting and retries.
  • Lock in a consistent order; back rules with constraints.
  • Keep transactions short: hold a reservation, never a lock, while waiting on payments.

callout.text: Next up: Files & Media — where photos and videos go instead of the database, and how they get there and back.

files.title: Files & Media
files.summary: Photos and videos don’t belong in your database — where they go instead, and how they get there and back.

goals.text: Bytes in object storage, metadata in the database
Direct uploads with presigned URLs; big files in parts
Processing, CDN delivery and adaptive video
Keeping metadata and files in step
Storage classes, lifecycle and private buckets

steps.title: Photos in the database
body: The PhotoShare app from Napkin Math started simply: an uploaded photo is saved as a BLOB — a binary column — right next to its caption, owner and date. One database, one backup, one place to look.
For the first few thousand users it works perfectly well.

callout.text: A photo is a few megabytes; the facts about it — owner, size, caption, when — are a few hundred bytes. They are very different kinds of data.

steps.title: Two terabytes a day
body: Now a million photos a day arrive at 2 MB each: 2 TB a day, 730 TB in a year. The database, its replicas and its backups all grow by that much. A restore takes days, and every new replica has to copy everything.
Every photo view also travels through the app servers and the database. Images push the useful rows out of the database’s memory, and queries for captions and likes slow down.

callout.text: Databases are built to search and update small records. Shipping megabytes in and out is expensive work that only gets in the way.

changes: − Photo views crowd out everything else

steps.title: Bytes in object storage, facts in the database
body: Move the bytes to object storage — Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob Storage. It is a huge key → file store: PUT a file under a key like photos/9f2c.jpg, GET it back. No queries, no joins — and no practical size limit.
It copies every object across several data centres for you and costs far less per terabyte than database disks. The database keeps one small row per photo: its key, owner, size and type.

callout.text: This split — metadata in a database, bytes in object storage — is how almost every product stores files, from profile pictures to multi-gigabyte videos.

changes: ~ Database keeps one ~1 KB row per photo
~ Database growth 2 TB → 1 GB a day

steps.title: Case: a 2 GB video over a phone connection
body: Uploads still flow through the app servers on their way to storage. A 2 GB video from a phone takes minutes, and the whole time it holds a server connection and memory open — just to pass bytes along.
The app servers end up sized for bandwidth rather than for the logic they actually run, and a burst of video uploads slows everyone’s page loads.

callout.text: If your servers only relay bytes they don’t look at, they are an expensive middle-man.

changes: − Each upload holds an app server for minutes

steps.title: Upload straight to storage
body: Instead, the app hands out permission and gets out of the way. The phone asks “may I upload a 2 GB video?”; the app checks the user, writes a pending row, and replies with a presigned URL: a link signed with the app’s key that allows one upload, to one key, for the next 15 minutes.
The phone sends the bytes directly to object storage. When the upload finishes, storage sends an event and the app marks the row uploaded.

callout.text: The signature can also pin the content type and a maximum size, so the URL can’t be reused to dump anything else into your bucket.

card.title: A presigned upload
lines: # the app never touches the bytes

steps.title: Big files: upload in parts
body: One 2 GB request over a phone network rarely makes it in one piece. A multipart upload splits the file into parts — say 10 MB each — sent in parallel, each with its own presigned URL.
A part that fails is simply sent again; a dropped connection resumes from the last part that arrived. When every part is in, one final call stitches them into a single object.

callout.text: Parallel parts are also faster: several connections fill a link better than one. Remove abandoned, half-finished uploads automatically, or you pay to store their parts.

changes: + Failed parts retried on their own
+ Uploads resume after a dropped connection

card.title: Multipart upload
lines: part 1…200  10 MB each, 4 at a time

steps.title: Make the versions people actually download
body: An original is rarely what you show. Each “upload complete” event goes onto a queue (see Message Queues), and workers make what the app needs: thumbnails and two or three sizes of each photo, a scan for malware, and — before anything is shared — removal of the GPS location hidden in the photo’s metadata.
Videos are transcoded into several resolutions. When a worker finishes, it saves the new files and marks the row ready; until then the app shows “processing…”.

callout.text: Never trust an upload. Check the real file type, size and content in the workers, not just what the client claimed.

steps.title: Serve them from the edge
body: Downloads far outnumber uploads, so they must not come through the app either. Photos are served by a CDN (see Content Delivery) with object storage as its origin: the first viewer in a city pulls a copy to the nearest edge, everyone after gets it from there.
Give each version a key that changes when its content does — photos/9f2c_w640.webp — and it can be cached for a year without ever going stale.

callout.text: For private photos, the app hands out short-lived signed CDN URLs — the same idea as presigned uploads, in the other direction.

changes: + CDN in front of object storage
~ Views served from the nearest edge

steps.title: Video: let the player choose
body: A video file is too big to download before playing, and viewers’ connections vary from second to second. So each video is cut into segments of a few seconds, encoded at several qualities — 240p up to 1080p — with a small playlist file listing them all.

The player fetches segment by segment from the CDN and picks the quality for the next one from how fast the last one arrived. A train enters a tunnel: the picture drops to 360p instead of freezing. This is adaptive bitrate streaming (HLS or DASH).

callout.text: Small, separately cacheable segments are also what makes video work so well on CDNs: every popular segment ends up at every edge.

changes: + Player switches quality segment by segment

steps.title: Case: rows without files, files without rows
body: Two stores can disagree. A phone gets its presigned URL and then loses signal: the row says pending for ever. A user deletes a photo: the row goes, but the files stay — still costing money, and still reachable by anyone who kept the link.

Fix it like any two-system update (see Sagas): every row has a status; storage events move it forward; deletes remove the row first and queue the file deletions; and a nightly cleanup job clears pending rows older than a day and files that no row points to.

callout.text: Deleting user data is a legal duty in many places. Make sure deletion reaches every copy: sizes, transcodes, backups and the CDN.

changes: + Status on every row: pending → uploaded → ready
+ Deletes: row first, then queued file deletes

steps.title: Old files can live somewhere cheaper
body: Most photos are looked at in their first few weeks and hardly ever again. Object stores sell storage classes: standard for hot data, “infrequent access” for less, and archive tiers that cost a fraction as much — but charge more, or take minutes to hours, to read.
A lifecycle rule moves objects automatically: originals older than 90 days go to an archive tier, while the small sizes people still browse stay hot.

callout.text: Cheap storage with expensive reads is a trap for data you still read often. Check how your files are actually accessed before archiving them.

changes: ~ Storage bill after one year $16,800 → ≈ $6,300 / month

card.title: Storage classes · per TB-month
lines: archive             ≈ $1–4   slow or costly to read

steps.title: Case: the bucket anyone can list
body: A developer makes the bucket public “to get images showing”. Months later someone discovers they can list it — and download every photo ever uploaded, including private ones and the originals with their location data. Leaks like this are among the most common cloud breaches.

Keep buckets private and block public access at the account level. Serve through the CDN with signed URLs, give each service a key that can touch only its own paths, and use unguessable object names as a last line, not the only one.

callout.text: A random key is not access control. If a URL is all it takes to read a private file, that URL must expire.

changes: + Public access blocked, CDN with signed URLs

steps.title: Recap
body:
• Bytes in object storage, metadata in the database — joined by the object’s key.
  • Clients upload directly with presigned URLs; big files go in parts that can be retried and resumed.
  • Workers make thumbnails, sizes and transcodes — and strip what shouldn’t be shared.
  • Serve through a CDN with versioned keys; stream video in adaptive segments.
  • Keep rows and files in step, move old files to cheaper classes, and keep buckets private.

callout.text: That completes Data & Storage. Next module: Communication — how services talk to each other.

apis.title: REST, RPC & GraphQL
apis.summary: Three ways for programs to ask each other for things — and what each costs a phone on 4G.

goals.text: GraphQL: ask for exactly what you need

steps.title: Programs need a contract
body: Your mobile app shows a profile: name, avatar, the last three posts and a follower count. The data lives on your servers, so the app has to ask for it.
An API is the agreed way to ask: which addresses exist, what to send, and what comes back. Here it’s JSON over HTTPS.

callout.text: An API is a promise. Once apps depend on it, changing it without breaking them is a real design problem.

steps.title: REST: resources and verbs
body: REST treats data as resources with addresses — /users/42, /users/42/posts — and uses HTTP verbs on them: GET to read, POST to create, PUT/PATCH to update, DELETE to remove.

It’s simple, works with every tool, and GET responses can be cached by browsers and CDNs. GET, PUT and DELETE are also idempotent — repeating one changes nothing more — while POST is not, which matters the moment a client retries.

callout.text: Status codes carry meaning too: 200 OK, 201 Created, 404 Not Found, 429 Too Many Requests, 500 server error.

changes: + Three endpoints for the profile screen

steps.title: Chatty and bloated on a phone
body: On a phone, each round trip costs about 100 ms. The client makes its three calls one after another — often it has to, because one call needs an id from the previous answer — so the screen waits for all three in a row.
Each endpoint also returns the whole object: 48 KB arrive to show about 3 KB. That’s over-fetching; needing several calls for one screen is under-fetching.

callout.text: Round trips and wasted bytes hurt most where networks are slowest — exactly where mobile users are.

steps.title: GraphQL: ask for exactly what you need
body: With GraphQL, the client sends one query describing the exact shape it wants. The GraphQL server fetches each part from the services behind it and returns just those fields.
Watch one request leave the phone, split to the Users and Posts services, and come back as one response.

callout.text: Great when many different clients (iOS, Android, web, TV) each need slightly different data from the same backend.

changes: + Users and Posts services behind it

steps.title: Flexible queries can be expensive
body: Clients can ask for anything the schema allows — including followers of followers of followers, with all their posts. One innocent-looking query (the big square) melts the Users service.
And because queries are normally sent as a POST to a single URL, ordinary HTTP caches and CDNs can’t help without extra work such as persisted queries.

callout.text: Production GraphQL needs query depth and cost limits, and often an allow-list of approved (“persisted”) queries.

steps.title: Inside the data center: RPC
body: Behind the API, services call each other constantly. Here the usual choice is RPC (remote procedure call): calling a function on another machine as if it were local — today usually gRPC.
The contract is a typed schema (Protocol Buffers); code for both sides is generated from it, and messages travel as compact binary over HTTP/2.

callout.text: gRPC is fast and strictly typed, and supports streaming — but browsers can’t speak it natively (they need a gRPC-Web proxy), so it mostly stays inside your network.

card.title: A gRPC contract
lines: = binary · typed · a few × smaller than JSON

steps.title: Case: a list with 2 million items
body: A celebrity’s followers list has 2 million entries. Returning it in one response would mean hundreds of megabytes and a very long wait. APIs return lists in pages.

?offset=40000&limit=20 looks simple, but the database still walks past 40,000 rows. A cursor — “the 20 after id 9f3c” — jumps straight there with an index, and doesn’t skip or repeat items when new ones arrive.

callout.text: Return the cursor for the next page in each response. Clients just pass it back.

steps.title: Case: renaming a field breaks old apps
body: A tidy-up renames name to display_name. The new app is fine — but millions of phones still run last year’s version, and their profile screens now crash.

Mobile apps can’t be forced to update. So APIs evolve additively: add the new field, keep the old one, and only remove it once almost nobody calls it. For truly breaking changes, publish a new version (/v2/) and run both.

callout.text: Once an API is public, every field is a promise. Measure who uses it before you break it.

card.title: Evolving safely
lines: ! remove or rename a field   → old apps break

steps.title: Which one, where?
body:
Best forWatch out
RESTPublic APIs, simple CRUD, cachingMany calls per screen
GraphQLMany clients, varied screensCostly queries, caching
gRPCService-to-serviceNot for browsers
They mix happily: REST or GraphQL at the edge for clients, gRPC between services inside.

callout.text: Whatever the style, version your API and never break existing clients — add fields, don’t rename or remove them.

steps.title: Recap
body:
• An API is a contract between programs.
  • REST: resources + HTTP verbs; simple and cacheable, but chatty for rich screens.
  • GraphQL: one query, exact fields; guard against expensive queries.
  • gRPC: fast, typed calls between internal services.
  • Page long lists with cursors; evolve APIs additively.

callout.text: Next up: Message Queues — for work that shouldn’t make anyone wait for an answer.

queues.title: Message Queues
queues.summary: Answer right away, do the slow work later — and never lose a job along the way.

goals.text: Why slow work doesn’t belong in a request

steps.title: Slow work inside the request
body: Creators upload videos, and each one must be transcoded into several sizes — about 30 seconds of heavy work. Right now the web server does it inside the upload request.
So the creator stares at a spinner for 30 s, many requests time out, and while servers grind through videos, every other page on the site slows down too.

callout.text: Anything slow, heavy or unreliable inside a request — video, email, reports, third-party calls — makes users wait for it.

steps.title: Put a queue in between
body: The web server now just stores the upload, puts a small job message on a message queue, and replies at once: “processing — we’ll notify you”.
Separate worker machines pull jobs off the queue and transcode at their own pace. The web server is the producer; workers are consumers.

callout.text: Popular queues: RabbitMQ, Amazon SQS, Google Pub/Sub, and Kafka (a log that also works as a queue).

steps.title: A spike becomes a backlog
body: A big creator goes live and uploads jump tenfold. Without the queue, that spike would have flattened the web servers.
Now the web tier stays fast — it only enqueues — and jobs simply wait their turn. Workers keep a steady pace and catch up after the rush.

callout.text: A queue turns “too much work right now” into “a bit more waiting later”. This is called load levelling.

steps.title: Add workers to drain it
body: Need to catch up faster? Start more workers. They all pull from the same queue, and each job goes to exactly one of them — the competing consumers pattern.
Workers are stateless, so adding them is easy, and many teams scale them automatically on queue length.

callout.text: Producers and consumers now scale independently: add web servers for traffic, workers for processing.

steps.title: A worker dies mid-job
body: A worker crashes halfway through transcoding. If the queue deleted each job the moment it handed it out, that video is simply gone — the creator waits forever.
Machines crash, get restarted and are replaced all the time. The queue has to assume it.

callout.text: Handing out a job is not the same as finishing it.

steps.title: Acknowledge when done
body: Fix: a job is only hidden while a worker has it. When the worker finishes, it sends an acknowledgement and the job is deleted. No ack within a timeout? The job reappears and another worker picks it up.
The catch: a job can now run twice (say, a worker finishes but dies before acking). So jobs must be idempotent — safe to repeat.

callout.text: This is “at-least-once” delivery, the norm for queues. Exactly-once is very hard; idempotent consumers get you the same result.

card.title: Acknowledgements
lines: 1. worker takes a job → hidden, not deleted
3. no ack in 60 s → visible again
! may run twice → make jobs idempotent

steps.title: Poison messages and the dead-letter queue
body: One upload is a corrupt file. Every worker that tries it crashes or fails, the job is redelivered, and it fails again — forever, wasting workers and blocking others.
So queues count attempts. After, say, 3 failures the message is moved to a dead-letter queue (DLQ) for a human or a script to inspect.

callout.text: Alert on DLQ size. A growing dead-letter queue is often the first sign of a bug.

changes: ~ Failing jobs moved aside after 3 attempts

steps.title: Case: messages out of order
body: A different queue carries account events: created, email changed, deleted. With several workers pulling in parallel, a slow worker can finish “email changed” after another worker has already processed “deleted”.
Many queues give no ordering guarantee at all — and even ordered ones lose it once several consumers work in parallel.

callout.text: If correctness depends on order, you must design for it explicitly.

steps.title: Order per key with partitions
body: Systems like Kafka split a topic into partitions. Messages with the same key (say, the account id) always go to the same partition, and each partition is read by one worker, in order.
So events for one account stay in order, while different accounts are still processed in parallel across partitions.

callout.text: Order is guaranteed per key, not globally. Global order means one consumer — and no parallelism.

changes: ~ Events per account stay in order

steps.title: When the backlog never drains
body: Queues absorb spikes — but if jobs arrive faster than workers finish them for hours, the backlog grows forever. Jobs get older and older, and eventually storage runs out.
Watch queue age, not just length, and push back: autoscale workers, cap the queue, and tell producers to slow down (or reject new jobs with a clear “try later”).

callout.text: A queue buys time, not capacity. Long-term, throughput must match the arrival rate.

changes: + Queue capped · producers told to retry later

steps.title: Recap
body:
• Move slow work out of the request: enqueue a job and answer immediately.
  • Queues absorb spikes; add workers to drain the backlog.
  • Ack after finishing; unacked jobs are retried — keep jobs idempotent.
  • Park repeat failures in a dead-letter queue.
  • Keep order per key with partitions; watch queue age and push back.

callout.text: Next up: Pub/Sub & Events — when one thing happening should trigger many others.

pubsub.title: Pub/Sub & Events
pubsub.summary: Announce that something happened, and let whoever cares react — without anyone waiting.

goals.text: Why direct calls couple services together
The outbox pattern and replaying events

steps.title: Checkout calls everyone
body: When an order is placed, four other things must happen: send a confirmation email, reserve stock, record analytics, add loyalty points.
The order service calls each of them in turn and waits for every answer, so the shopper waits for all four — almost a second.

callout.text: Every new feature that cares about orders means changing, testing and redeploying the order service.

steps.title: Email is down, so nobody can buy
body: The email provider has an outage. The order service’s call to it fails — and because checkout waits on every call, checkout fails.
A confirmation email, which could easily have been sent ten minutes later, just stopped all sales.

callout.text: With direct calls, availability multiplies: four services at 99.9% each give checkout about 99.6%.

steps.title: Publish an event instead
body: The order service now saves the order and publishes one event — OrderPlaced — to a topic on an event bus, then answers the shopper straight away.
Email, inventory, analytics and loyalty each subscribe to the topic, and every one of them receives its own copy of the event.

callout.text: Common brokers: Kafka, Amazon SNS + SQS, Google Pub/Sub, RabbitMQ (fanout exchanges), Redis Streams.

steps.title: Queue or topic?
body: In the last lesson, each job went to one worker — a queue shares out work. A topic does the opposite: each event goes to every subscriber — it spreads news.
Real systems combine them: each subscribing service gets its own queue of events, shared by however many instances of that service are running.

callout.text: Queue: “someone do this.” Topic: “this happened.”

card.title: Queue vs topic
lines: queue → each message to ONE consumer
topic → each message to EVERY subscriber

steps.title: New features just subscribe
body: The risk team wants to check every order for fraud. They build a service that subscribes to OrderPlaced — and that’s it.
The order service didn’t change, wasn’t redeployed, and doesn’t even know fraud checking exists. This is loose coupling.

callout.text: Publishers don’t know their subscribers. Teams can add reactions to events without coordinating releases.

steps.title: A subscriber is down? It catches up
body: Email is down again. This time checkout doesn’t notice: the event bus keeps email’s copies of the events in its subscription until it’s back.
When email recovers, it works through the backlog and every confirmation goes out — a little late, but none lost.

callout.text: Events are durable: a slow or broken subscriber delays only itself.

changes: + Its events wait in its subscription

steps.title: What events cost
body: Events decouple services, but the flow becomes harder to see: “what happens when an order is placed?” is now spread across five codebases.
Subscribers act a little later (eventual consistency), events can arrive twice or out of order, and debugging needs good tracing.

callout.text: Name events as facts in the past tense (OrderPlaced, PaymentFailed), and make every subscriber idempotent.

card.title: Events: the fine print
lines: who reacts to OrderPlaced? check 5 repos

steps.title: Case: saved, but never announced
body: The order service saves the order to its database, then publishes OrderPlaced. One day it crashes between those two steps: the order exists, but no event was sent. No email, no stock reserved, no loyalty points.
Fix: the transactional outbox. Write the event into an outbox table in the same database transaction as the order; a relay then publishes everything in the outbox to the bus.

callout.text: Either both the order and its event are saved, or neither is. The relay retries until the bus accepts it — so subscribers must handle duplicates. It can poll the table, or tail the database’s own log (change data capture, e.g. Debezium).

changes: + Orders DB with an outbox table
~ No more lost events after a crash

steps.title: Case: replaying history
body: Analytics finds a bug that miscounted revenue for the last 30 days. With a classic queue, those events are gone once consumed.
A log-based bus like Kafka keeps events for days or weeks. Analytics fixes its code, rewinds its position to 30 days ago, and reprocesses every event — other subscribers aren’t affected.

callout.text: Retained events also let a brand-new subscriber build its data from history instead of starting empty.

steps.title: Recap
body:
• Direct calls make the caller slow and fragile, and couple every team to it.
  • Publish an event; every subscriber gets its own copy.
  • New features just subscribe; down subscribers catch up later.
  • Pay for it with eventual consistency, duplicates and harder tracing.
  • Use an outbox so saves and events never disagree; retained logs allow replay.

callout.text: Next up: Real-time Updates — getting events all the way to a user’s screen.

realtime.title: Real-time Updates
realtime.summary: How the server tells you something happened — chat, live scores, notifications.

goals.text: Why HTTP can’t push on its own

steps.title: Bob sent a message. How does Alice find out?
body: Bob’s message reaches the chat server. Alice’s phone should show it instantly.
But plain HTTP is request → response: only the client can start a conversation. The server has no way to call Alice’s phone and say “you’ve got mail”.

callout.text: Phones and browsers sit behind home routers and mobile networks that block incoming connections — the client has to reach out.

steps.title: Polling: keep asking
body: The simplest fix: Alice’s app asks “anything new?” every 2 seconds. Most answers are empty (pale dots); now and then one carries a message (green).
Easy to build with ordinary requests — but messages arrive up to 2 seconds late, and most requests are wasted.

callout.text: Polling is fine for things that change slowly — a build status, an order tracking page — with a sensible interval.

steps.title: Polling a million phones
body: Now multiply. A million users each asking every 2 seconds is half a million requests per second — and 95% of them get the answer “nothing new”.
You’d be paying for a fleet of servers whose main job is saying no. Polling faster to cut the delay makes it worse.

callout.text: Polling trades freshness against load: halve the delay, double the requests.

steps.title: Long polling: hold the request open
body: Instead of answering “nothing” immediately, the server holds the request open (watch the request wait at the server) until a message arrives, or about 30 seconds pass. Then it responds, and the app immediately asks again.
Messages now arrive almost instantly, and empty answers are rare.

callout.text: Long polling works anywhere plain HTTP works, so it’s still used as a fallback when nothing better is available.

changes: ~ Server holds each request until there’s news
~ Delay up to 2 s → under 100 ms

steps.title: Server-Sent Events: one response that never ends
body: With Server-Sent Events (SSE), the app makes one request and the server never finishes the response. Instead, it writes each new event down that open stream as it happens.
It’s one-way (server → client), plain HTTP, and browsers reconnect automatically. Alice still sends her own messages with normal requests.

callout.text: Ideal for feeds, notifications, live scores and dashboards — and for streaming AI responses token by token.

changes: + One long-lived event stream to Alice

steps.title: WebSockets: talk both ways
body: A WebSocket starts as an HTTP request, then upgrades into a permanent two-way connection. Either side can send a message at any moment, with tiny overhead per message.
Bob and Alice each hold one socket; messages flow both ways through the server in a few milliseconds.

callout.text: Use WebSockets when the client talks back often: chat, multiplayer games, collaborative editing, trading screens.

changes: ~ Sending no longer needs separate requests

steps.title: Scaling: which server has Alice?
body: Each open connection costs memory, so a million users need many chat servers. Now Bob’s socket is on server 2, but Alice’s is on server 1 — server 2 can’t deliver to her directly.
So servers relay through pub/sub: server 2 publishes to Alice’s channel, and whichever server holds her socket is subscribed and forwards it. Watch a message take the long way round.

callout.text: This is the previous lesson again — pub/sub is how real-time systems fan messages out across servers.

changes: ~ Messages relayed to the server holding each socket

steps.title: Case: Alice’s phone is offline
body: Alice goes into the subway. Her socket drops, and Bob’s messages have nowhere to go.

So every message is first saved to a store, then pushed if the recipient is connected. When Alice reconnects, her app says “I last saw message 1041” and fetches everything after it. If she stays offline, a mobile push notification (APNs, FCM) wakes her phone.

callout.text: Real-time delivery is an optimisation. The stored message, fetched on reconnect, is the source of truth.

changes: + Catch up on reconnect · push notification

steps.title: Presence: who’s online
body: The green dot next to a name needs presence: each app sends a small heartbeat every 30 seconds, and the server records “last seen”. No heartbeat for a minute means offline.
With a million users that’s ~33,000 heartbeats a second. Keep presence in a fast store with expiring keys, and only push changes to people who are actually looking at that contact.

callout.text: Presence is approximate by design — a few seconds of delay is fine, and it saves enormous traffic.

steps.title: Recap
body:
DelayDirection
PollingUp to the intervalClient asks
Long pollingLowClient asks, server waits
SSELowServer → client
WebSocketLowestBoth ways
Persistent connections need many servers at scale, joined by pub/sub. Store every message first, so offline users catch up when they return.

callout.text: That completes Communication. Next module: Reliability — starting with redundancy and failover.

redundancy.title: Redundancy & Failover
redundancy.summary: Everything fails eventually. Design so that no single failure takes you down.

goals.text: Find and remove single points of failure

steps.title: How available is one of everything?
body: A simple stack: a load balancer, an app server and a database. Each one is up 99.9% of the time — that sounds great.
But a request needs all three working, so their availabilities multiply: 0.999 × 0.999 × 0.999 ≈ 99.7%. That’s about 26 hours of downtime a year.

callout.text: Availability is usually quoted in “nines”. Each extra nine cuts allowed downtime by 10×.

steps.title: Every box is a single point of failure
body: A single point of failure (SPOF) is anything whose failure alone takes the system down. Here, that’s every component.
A bad disk, a kernel panic, a botched deploy — any one of them and a million users see an error page.

callout.text: Hardware fails, software crashes and people make mistakes. Assume each will happen — the question is what breaks when it does.

steps.title: Redundancy: two of everything
body: Add a spare for each part: the load balancer runs as an active–passive pair, two app servers share traffic, and the database has a follower ready to take over.
Now both copies must fail at once for an outage — 0.1% × 0.1% = 0.0001%. Losing any single machine is a non-event.

callout.text: On paper, parts in parallel multiply their failure chances: two 99.9% copies give 99.9999%. Real pairs do worse — failover takes time, and both copies still share a building, a network and your deploys — so we count a cautious 99.95%.

steps.title: Copies that fail together
body: All those copies sit in one data center. Then a power outage (or a flood, a fibre cut, a cooling failure) takes out the whole building — and every “redundant” copy with it.
Failures that hit many components at once are correlated failures. Redundancy only helps if the copies fail independently.

callout.text: Shared power, network, racks, software versions and even the same bad config push can all take out every copy together.

steps.title: Spread across availability zones
body: Cloud regions are split into availability zones: separate data centers, kilometres to tens of kilometres apart, with their own power and network, joined by fast links.
Put one app server and one database copy in each zone. A zone-wide disaster now takes out only half.

callout.text: Same idea at every scale: spread across racks, zones and — for the most critical systems — whole regions.

changes: ~ One copy of each tier per zone

steps.title: Zone A goes dark — failover
body: Zone A loses power. Health checks fail, the load balancer stops sending traffic there, and the follower in zone B is promoted to leader.
Users in the middle of a request may see an error and retry; within a minute everything runs from zone B.

callout.text: Zone B must have enough spare capacity to carry all the traffic alone. Redundancy you can’t afford to run on is not redundancy.

steps.title: How fast, and how much lost?
body: Two numbers describe a failover. RTO (recovery time objective): how long until service is back. RPO (recovery point objective): how much recent data you can afford to lose.
Async replication means the follower may be a few seconds behind — those writes are gone. Synchronous replication gets RPO to zero, at the cost of slower writes.

callout.text: Decide RTO and RPO with the business first; they determine the design (and the bill).

card.title: This failover
lines: ! RPO ≈ 2 s of async writes lost

steps.title: Untested failover doesn’t work
body: A failover path that never runs quietly rots: a config drifts, a spare is too small, a script has a typo. You find out during the real outage.
So teams break things on purpose, in production, during working hours — chaos engineering. Here a test kills an app server and everyone watches the system cope.

callout.text: Netflix’s Chaos Monkey randomly kills servers every day. Start smaller: a planned game day, one failure at a time.

steps.title: Case: the bug that’s everywhere at once
body: A new release with a bug goes out to every app server in both zones at the same moment. Every copy crashes on the same request — redundancy doesn’t help when all the copies share the same broken code.
This is the most common cause of real outages: not hardware, but changes — code, config, or infrastructure.

callout.text: Identical copies fail identically. A bad change is a correlated failure you inflict on yourself.

changes: + Release v2.4 to all servers at once

steps.title: Canary releases
body: Roll out in stages instead. First a canary: one server, or 1% of traffic, gets v2.4. Watch its error rate and latency against the others for a while.
If it looks worse, roll back — only 1% of users were affected, briefly. If it looks good, continue to 10%, 50%, 100%. Many teams also deploy one zone at a time.

callout.text: Feature flags complement this: ship code turned off, then turn it on gradually — and off instantly if needed.

steps.title: Beyond zones: multiple regions
body: Zones protect against a building failing. A whole region can still go down (a regional network or cloud control-plane outage), and it’s far from users on other continents.
Running in two regions with a global DNS or anycast front door lets users go to the nearest healthy region. The hard part is the data: copies across an ocean replicate with ~100 ms of lag.

callout.text: Multi-region is expensive and complex. Most systems are well served by multiple zones in one region plus good backups.

changes: + Global front door routes to the nearest healthy region

steps.title: Recap
body:
• Components in a chain multiply their availability.
  • Remove single points of failure with redundant copies.
  • Copies must fail independently: spread them across zones.
  • Set RTO/RPO, and practise failover so it works when needed.
  • Most outages are changes: roll out with canaries.

callout.text: Next up: Rate Limiting — protecting the system from too much of the wrong traffic.

rate-limiting.title: Rate Limiting
rate-limiting.summary: Give every client a fair budget, so one runaway script can’t take everyone down.

goals.text: Why one client can starve everyone

steps.title: One script, everyone suffers
body: A customer’s script has a bug: it calls your API in a tight loop — 5,000 requests a second. The API servers spend almost all their time on it.
Real users’ requests queue behind the flood and time out. Nobody attacked you; one client simply took more than its share.

callout.text: Shared capacity needs a fairness rule. Without one, the noisiest client wins.

steps.title: A rate limiter at the front door
body: Put a rate limiter in the gateway in front of the API. Each client — identified by API key, user id or IP address — gets a budget, say 10 requests per second.
Requests within budget pass through. The rest are rejected immediately with 429 Too Many Requests, before they cost the API anything.

callout.text: Rejecting early is cheap: the gateway answers in microseconds, and the API never sees the excess.

steps.title: How it counts: the token bucket
body: The most common algorithm is the token bucket. Each client has a bucket holding up to 10 tokens, refilled at 10 per second. Every request takes a token; an empty bucket means 429.
A real user’s bucket stays mostly full (the green dots). The script empties its bucket instantly and stays empty.

callout.text: Bucket size allows short bursts; the refill rate caps the long-run average. Two numbers, easy to explain.

steps.title: Windows vs buckets
body: A simpler fixed window counts requests per calendar minute and resets at :00. Easy — but a client can send a full minute’s budget at 12:00:59 and again at 12:01:00: double the limit in two seconds.
A sliding window smooths that edge; a token bucket allows controlled bursts. Most API gateways use one of the latter two.

callout.text: Need a steady outflow instead (e.g. to a fragile partner API)? A leaky bucket queues requests and releases them at a fixed pace.

steps.title: Many gateways, one budget
body: One gateway isn’t enough, so you run several behind a load balancer. If each counts on its own, a client spread across 10 gateways gets 10× its limit.
So gateways keep the counters in a shared, fast store (often Redis): each request does an atomic increment and checks the total.

callout.text: The shared store adds ~1 ms per request. Some systems trade a little accuracy for speed by syncing local counters every second.

changes: − Per-client buckets now live in the store

steps.title: Tell clients how to behave
body: A good 429 says when to come back: a Retry-After: 30 header, plus headers showing the limit and what’s left. Well-behaved clients slow down and retry later.
The script’s owner fixes their loop. Now it uses its fair share and nothing more.

callout.text: Publish your limits in the API docs, and offer higher tiers for customers who genuinely need more.

steps.title: Case: one customer’s 10,000 users
body: You sell your API to companies. One customer runs a nightly import with 10,000 well-behaved users — each under their personal limit, but together using 70% of your capacity. Other customers slow down every night.
Per-user limits can’t see this. Add limits per tenant (customer account), sized by their plan, on top of per-user limits.

callout.text: Layer limits: per user, per tenant, per endpoint (expensive endpoints get lower limits), and a global ceiling.

changes: ~ Big import capped at its plan’s share

steps.title: When everyone spikes: shed load
body: Rate limits stop one client hogging capacity. But on launch day everyone arrives at once and the total is still more than you can serve.
Then load shedding decides what to drop: background work like prefetching, recommendations and analytics (amber) is rejected first, so logins and checkouts keep working.

callout.text: Failing some requests on purpose beats failing all of them by accident.

changes: + Low-priority requests shed at the gateway

steps.title: Recap
body:
• Give each client a budget; reject the excess early with 429.
  • Token buckets allow short bursts and cap the average rate.
  • Across many gateways, keep counters in a shared store.
  • Layer limits: per user, per tenant, per endpoint.
  • Under global overload, shed low-priority work first.

callout.text: Next up: Timeouts & Retries — what to do when the service you’re calling is the one in trouble.

timeouts-retries.title: Timeouts & Retries
timeouts-retries.summary: Calling a struggling service safely: give up in time, retry carefully, and know when to stop.

goals.text: How one slow service spreads failure
Retries, retry storms and backoff with jitter

steps.title: One slow service takes down another
body: The payment service starts answering in 30 seconds instead of 50 ms. The order service calls it and simply waits — with no limit.
Each waiting call holds a thread. Within a minute all 200 are stuck, and the order service can’t even serve pages that don’t need payments. A slow dependency became a full outage.

callout.text: This is a cascading failure: trouble spreads upstream through anything that waits without a limit.

steps.title: Set a timeout, have a fallback
body: Give every outgoing call a timeout: if payments hasn’t answered in 800 ms, give up and free the thread.
Then degrade gracefully: accept the order as “payment pending” and charge it shortly after. The order service stays up for everything else.

callout.text: Set timeouts from real latency: a bit above the dependency’s p99, and always shorter than your own caller’s timeout.

steps.title: Retry the blips
body: Many failures are momentary: a dropped packet, a server restarting, a brief hiccup. Trying again a moment later usually works.
One retry (amber) turns most of those failures into successes.

callout.text: Only retry errors that might succeed next time — timeouts, 503s. Retrying a 400 Bad Request just fails again.

steps.title: Retries become a storm
body: Then payments gets genuinely overloaded. Every caller retries — three times, immediately. Each failed request becomes four, so the struggling service now gets 4× its normal load.
It can never recover: the retries themselves keep it down. Your clients have turned into a denial-of-service attack.

callout.text: Retries multiply across layers too: 3 retries at each of 3 layers is up to 64 calls for one click.

steps.title: Back off, with jitter
body: Wait before retrying, and wait longer each time: 100 ms, then 200, then 400 — exponential backoff. Add randomness (jitter) so thousands of clients don’t retry in the same instant.
Cap the attempts, and cap the share of traffic that may be retries (a retry budget of ~10%). Payments gets room to recover.

callout.text: Most cloud SDKs already do exponential backoff with jitter — check that it’s on, and that layers don’t stack their retries.

steps.title: Circuit breaker: stop calling for a while
body: Payments goes fully down. Even with timeouts, every call wastes 800 ms finding that out. A circuit breaker watches the failures — past a threshold it opens and fails calls instantly, without trying.
Every 30 seconds it lets one trial call through (half-open, the green ping). If that succeeds, it closes again.

callout.text: Like the breaker in your house: it trips to protect the rest of the system, and you reset it once the fault is fixed.

changes: ~ Failed calls take 1 ms, not 800 ms

steps.title: Half-open, then closed
body: Payments recovers. The next trial call succeeds, so the breaker closes and traffic flows again — gradually, so the service isn’t flooded the moment it’s back.
Meanwhile the “payment pending” orders are charged from a queue. No order was lost, and the rest of the site never went down.

callout.text: Libraries such as resilience4j, Polly and service meshes like Envoy/Istio provide timeouts, retries and breakers out of the box.

steps.title: Retries must not charge twice
body: A nasty case: payments charges the card, but the response is lost on the way back. The order service times out and retries — and the customer is charged twice.
Fix: send an idempotency key — a unique id per order — with every attempt. Payments remembers the result for each key and returns it again for duplicates instead of charging again.

callout.text: Any operation that may be retried must be idempotent: doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once.

changes: ~ Duplicate attempts return the stored result

steps.title: Pass the deadline along
body: The shopper’s browser gives up after 2 seconds. But if the order service has already spent 1.8 s, it’s pointless for payments to start a fresh 800 ms of work — nobody will see the answer.
So each request carries a deadline: “answer by 12:00:02.000”. Every service checks the time left and passes the remaining budget on; with none left, it stops immediately.

callout.text: gRPC propagates deadlines automatically. Over HTTP, pass the remaining time in a header.

changes: ~ No work started that can’t finish in time

steps.title: Bulkheads: separate pools
body: Remember step 1, when slow payments used up all 200 threads? The order service can also protect itself by giving each dependency its own pool: say 40 threads for payments, 40 for inventory, the rest for everything else.
Now when payments is slow, only its 40 threads fill up. Browsing, search and the cart keep working. Like the watertight compartments in a ship — the bulkhead pattern.

callout.text: Timeouts limit how long one call can hurt you; bulkheads limit how many calls can.

changes: ~ Slow payments fills only its 40 threads

steps.title: Recap
body:
• Every remote call needs a timeout and a fallback.
  • Retry transient errors — with exponential backoff, jitter and a cap.
  • A circuit breaker stops hammering a service that is down.
  • Retried operations must be idempotent.
  • Propagate deadlines; isolate dependencies with bulkheads.

callout.text: Next up: Observability — how you’d find out payments was slow in the first place.

observability.title: Observability
observability.summary: Metrics, logs and traces: how to find out what’s wrong, where, and why — fast.

goals.text: Why “it’s slow” is hard to debug
Handling an incident, and the post-mortem

steps.title: “Checkout is slow.” Where?
body: Support tickets pile up: checkout takes several seconds. A checkout touches the gateway, orders, inventory, payments, a database and a third-party fraud API.
You can see a request waiting somewhere in this diagram — but the team can’t. Every server’s CPU looks fine, and nobody knows where to start.

callout.text: If users find problems before you do, you are flying blind.

steps.title: Metrics: numbers over time
body: Every service records a few numbers about the requests it handles — the RED method: Rate (requests/s), Errors (failed share) and Duration (latency percentiles) — and sends them to a time-series store with dashboards.
Now the picture is clear: inventory and the database are fast; the slowness lives on the payments path.

callout.text: Common stacks: Prometheus + Grafana, Datadog, CloudWatch. Measure p99, not just averages. RED describes requests; for machines, watch USE: utilization, saturation, errors.

steps.title: Alert on what users feel
body: Don’t page people for “CPU above 80%” — it fires constantly and often means nothing. Alert on symptoms users feel.
Pick an SLI (say, the share of checkouts faster than 1 s), set an SLO target (99.9%), and alert when you’re burning through the remaining error budget too fast.

callout.text: An error budget turns reliability into a shared number: while it lasts, ship features; when it’s gone, fix reliability first.

steps.title: Logs: the story, line by line
body: Metrics say where; logs say what happened. Each service writes timestamped events — but at thousands of requests a second, lines from different requests interleave into noise.
The trick: give every request an id at the gateway, pass it along, and include it in every log line. Filter by one id and you get one request’s story.

callout.text: Log structured JSON, not free text — so you can filter by request id, user, service or status.

changes: + Request id on every log line

steps.title: Traces: follow one request everywhere
body: A distributed trace records every hop of one request as a span with a start time and duration, all joined by the same trace id. Drawn as a waterfall, it shows exactly where the time goes.
Follow the violet request: 2.1 of its 2.4 seconds are spent waiting for the third-party fraud API.

callout.text: Tools: OpenTelemetry to collect, Jaeger, Tempo, Honeycomb or Datadog to explore. Instrument once, use everywhere.

changes: ~ Cause found: fraud API ≈ 88% of the time

steps.title: Fix it, then prove it
body: With the cause known, the fix is quick: call the fraud API with a 300 ms timeout, cache recent scores, and review the rare slow cases afterwards.
The same dashboards prove it worked: p99 drops from 2.4 s to 310 ms, and the SLO alert clears. Total time from page to cause: minutes, not hours.

callout.text: Metrics tell you something is wrong, traces show where, logs explain why. You need all three.

changes: + 300 ms timeout + cache on fraud checks

steps.title: Case: 3 a.m. — errors spike
body: The pager fires: checkout errors jumped from 0.1% to 6% at 03:12. Inventory is the culprit on the dashboard. The deploy log shows a config change to inventory at 03:10.
Good practice is to mitigate first: roll the change back and restore service, and investigate the root cause afterwards — not the other way round.

callout.text: Put deploys and config changes on your dashboards as markers. “What changed?” is the first question in almost every incident.

steps.title: Learn from it: the post-mortem
body: After the incident, the team writes a post-mortem: a timeline, the impact, the root cause, and the actions that stop it happening again.
It’s blameless — the question is how the system let a mistake through, not who made it. Here: config changes now go through the same canary rollout as code.

callout.text: Each incident is expensive training data. Teams that write good post-mortems make the same mistake much less often.

changes: + Action: canary rollout for config too

card.title: Post-mortem · checkout errors
lines: cause: bad timeout in inventory config

steps.title: Recap
body:
• Metrics (rate, errors, duration) show where it hurts.
  • Alert on SLOs — what users feel — not on raw CPU.
  • Logs with a request id tell one request’s story.
  • Traces follow a request across every service.
  • In an incident, mitigate first; then write a blameless post-mortem.
Instrument before you need it — the outage is the wrong time to add logging.

callout.text: That completes Reliability. Next module: Architecture — starting with monoliths vs microservices.

microservices.title: Monolith vs Microservices
microservices.summary: One codebase or many services? What each buys you, what each costs, and how to move between them.

goals.text: What a monolith is good at — and where it hurts
The costs: a network in the middle
Queries across services: local read copies
Contract tests and the distributed monolith
Migrating safely with a strangler fig

steps.title: One app, one deploy
body: Your shop is a monolith: one codebase with every feature — accounts, catalog, orders, payments — deployed as one unit, several copies behind a load balancer, all sharing one database.
For a small team this is great: calls between features are plain function calls, one deploy ships everything, and a stack trace shows the whole story.

callout.text: Many very large companies ran on a monolith for years. It is a perfectly good architecture — until it isn’t.

steps.title: Fifty engineers, one codebase
body: The team grows to fifty people across six teams. Every change goes into one weekly release, so a bug in one feature delays everyone’s work.
A memory leak in the new reports feature crashes the whole process — checkout included. And to give search more memory, you must scale every copy of everything.

callout.text: The monolith’s problems are mostly about people: teams waiting on each other, and one team’s bug becoming everyone’s outage.

changes: ~ Scale everything to scale one feature

steps.title: Split by business capability
body: Break the app into microservices along business lines: Users, Catalog, Orders, Payments. Each is a separate program, owned by one team, deployed on its own schedule.
An API gateway gives clients one front door and routes each request to the right service.

callout.text: Split along business capabilities, not technical layers. A “database service” or “UI service” just moves the coupling around.

steps.title: Each service owns its data
body: If services still share one database, they are still tied together: a schema change by one team can break three others. So each service gets its own database, and nobody else touches it.
Need payment data in Orders? Ask Payments through its API — or listen to its events.

callout.text: Database per service is what makes independent deploys real. It also means no more joins or transactions across services — see the Sagas lesson.

card.title: Database per service
lines: = ask the owner: API or events
# each team picks its own store
