steps.title: The network is in the middle now
body: Showing one order page now takes several calls: gateway → Orders → Payments, plus Users and Catalog. Each hop adds latency, and each can be slow or fail on its own — watch one time out.
Debugging spans four codebases. You need timeouts, retries, tracing and good dashboards (the Reliability module) just to stay where the monolith started.

callout.text: A function call never fails halfway. A network call does — partially, slowly, and at the worst moment.

steps.title: Case: the distributed monolith
body: One company split its monolith into twelve services — but they kept reading each other’s tables, and every feature needed changes in five services released together.
They got the network costs of microservices and the coupling of a monolith. Releases got slower, not faster.

callout.text: If services must be deployed together, they are one service. Boundaries come first; the split comes second.

steps.title: Case: the order-history page
body: The order-history page shows each order with its product names and photos. In the monolith that was one SQL join. Now orders live in Orders and products in Catalog — and there are no joins across services.
So Orders calls Catalog once per order: 20 orders, 20 calls (the N+1 problem). The page is slow, and if Catalog is down, order history is down too.

callout.text: Screens that combine data from many services are where microservices hurt most. Plan for them up front.

steps.title: Keep a local read copy
body: Orders keeps its own copy of the few catalog fields it displays — name and photo — and Catalog publishes a ProductUpdated event whenever they change. Orders updates its copy from those events.
Order history is one query in Orders’ own database again, and it keeps working when Catalog is down. The price stays as it was at purchase anyway: it’s a historical fact, not a live lookup.

callout.text: The copy is eventually consistent: a renamed product shows the new name a moment later. For a history page, that’s fine.

changes: + Local copy of name and photo in Orders

steps.title: Case: an API change breaks a neighbour
body: The Payments team renames amount to amount_cents. Their own tests pass, they deploy — and every checkout in Orders starts failing. Independent deploys only work if teams can’t break each other by accident.

With consumer-driven contract tests, Orders publishes exactly which fields it relies on. Payments’ build runs those contracts before every release, and this change is blocked in CI instead of in production.

callout.text: Pair contracts with the API versioning rules from the REST lesson: add fields freely, remove them only when no contract needs them.

changes: + Orders publishes a contract for Payments’ API
~ Breaking change blocked in Payments’ CI

steps.title: Which one should you pick?
body:
MonolithMicroservices
Team sizeOne to a few teamsMany teams
DeploysTogetherIndependent
CallsIn-process, fastNetwork, can fail
DataOne DB, joins, transactionsDB per service, sagas
OpsSimpleNeeds good tooling
A common path: start with a modular monolith — one deployable with strict internal boundaries — and split out a module only when a team clearly needs independence.

callout.text: Microservices solve an organisational scaling problem. If you don’t have that problem yet, they mostly add cost.

steps.title: Migrating: the strangler fig
body: Don’t rewrite everything at once. Put the gateway in front of the monolith, build one new service — Payments — and route only /payments/* to it. Everything else still goes to the monolith.
Move one capability at a time until the monolith is small enough to retire. Each step is shippable and reversible.

callout.text: Named after the strangler fig, which grows around a tree until it can stand on its own.

changes: + Gateway in front of the monolith
+ New Payments service with its own DB

steps.title: Recap
body:
• A monolith is simple and fast — until many teams share it.
  • Microservices split by business capability, each with its own data.
  • You pay with network calls, partial failures and operational tooling.
  • Replace joins with local read copies; protect APIs with contract tests.
  • Avoid the distributed monolith; migrate gradually with a strangler fig.

callout.text: Next up: Service Discovery — how services find each other when instances come and go.

service-discovery.title: Service Discovery & Gateways
service-discovery.summary: How services find each other when instances come and go — and one front door for everyone outside.

goals.text: A registry that can’t go down

steps.title: Orders calls Payments
body: With microservices, Orders needs to call Payments. The simplest way: put the payment servers’ IP addresses in Orders’ config file and spread calls across them.
It works — as long as those two machines never change.

callout.text: In a monolith this question doesn’t exist: “calling payments” is a function call in the same process.

steps.title: Instances come and go
body: In the cloud, servers are cattle: the autoscaler adds and removes them, deploys replace them, crashed ones are swapped out. Instance 10.0.3.7 was just replaced by a new one at 10.0.5.21.
Orders still has the old list. Half its calls go to an address where nothing answers, while the new instance sits idle.

callout.text: Any address written into config goes stale. In an autoscaled system that can happen many times a day.

steps.title: A service registry
body: Every instance registers itself with a service registry when it starts, then keeps sending heartbeats (the green pings). Orders asks the registry “where is payments?” and gets the current list.
Popular registries: Consul, etcd, ZooKeeper, Eureka — and Kubernetes, which does this for every service automatically.

callout.text: Orders caches the list for a few seconds instead of asking on every call — the registry must not become a bottleneck.

steps.title: Instances join and leave by themselves
body: Now churn is harmless. A new instance (10.0.6.4) starts, registers, and gets traffic within seconds. Instance 10.0.5.21 hangs: it misses three heartbeats, and the registry drops it.
Nobody edited a config file.

callout.text: Heartbeats turn “is it alive?” into data the registry can act on — the same idea as load balancer health checks.

steps.title: Client-side or server-side?
body: Client-side discovery: Orders gets the list itself and picks an instance (round robin, least loaded). No extra hop, but every client needs that logic.
Server-side discovery: Orders calls one stable name, and an internal load balancer — or a Kubernetes Service — looks up the instances and forwards the call. Clients stay simple.

callout.text: Kubernetes gives every service a stable name and virtual IP; most teams never see the registry at all.

steps.title: Discovery through DNS
body: The registry can also answer through plain DNS: looking up payments.internal returns the healthy instances’ IPs. Every language and tool already speaks DNS.
The catch is caching: clients and libraries may keep an answer for its whole TTL (or longer), still calling an instance that has gone away. Keep TTLs short and retry on connection errors.

callout.text: Some runtimes cache DNS answers forever by default. Check yours before relying on DNS-based discovery.

steps.title: Case: traffic before it’s ready
body: A new instance registers the moment its process starts — before it has opened database connections or warmed its caches. The registry hands its address out at once, it gets a full share of traffic, and for 30 seconds a third of payment calls time out.
Being alive is not the same as being ready.

callout.text: Cold starts are worst right after deploys and autoscaling — exactly when traffic is moving around anyway.

steps.title: Readiness, slow start and draining
body: Separate two checks: liveness (“the process is running”) and readiness (“it can serve requests now”). An instance is only listed once it passes its readiness check, and balancers ramp its share up gradually — slow start.
Shutdown is the mirror image: deregister first, wait for in-flight requests to finish (draining), then stop.

callout.text: Kubernetes has these built in: readinessProbe, livenessProbe, and a preStop hook plus grace period for draining.

steps.title: What if the registry goes down?
body: Everything now depends on the registry, so it can’t be a single point of failure. Two things save you. Callers cache their last known list, so traffic keeps flowing even while the registry is unreachable — they just won’t see changes for a while.
And the registry runs as a small cluster of 3 or 5 nodes that agree by majority vote (Raft or Paxos). Losing one node — or even two out of five — changes nothing.

callout.text: etcd, Consul and ZooKeeper are all consensus clusters. Odd sizes matter: 3 nodes survive 1 failure, 5 survive 2.

steps.title: Every team rebuilds the same plumbing
body: Discovery is only the start. Every call between services also needs timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, encryption and metrics.
With services in Java, Go, Python and Node, each team writes its own version of all of that — with its own bugs, and its own defaults.

callout.text: Five implementations of retry logic means five different behaviours during an outage.

steps.title: A service mesh: sidecars do it
body: A service mesh (Istio, Linkerd) runs a small proxy — a sidecar — next to every service. Each service just talks to its local sidecar; the sidecars find instances, retry, time out, encrypt (mTLS) and report metrics.
A control plane pushes the current instances and policies to every sidecar. The plumbing is written once, in one place.

callout.text: A mesh adds latency (two extra local hops) and real operational complexity. Worth it with many services; overkill for a handful.

changes: + Sidecar proxy next to each service

steps.title: At the edge: an API gateway
body: Discovery handles calls between services. For clients outside — apps and browsers — an API gateway is the single front door: it authenticates requests, applies rate limits, terminates TLS and routes each path to the right service.
Clients never learn your internal layout, so you can split, merge or move services freely.

callout.text: Different clients often get their own gateway — a backend-for-frontend (BFF) — that shapes responses for mobile or web.

changes: + API gateway in front of the services

steps.title: Recap
body:
• Hard-coded addresses go stale as instances come and go.
  • A registry with heartbeats (or DNS) keeps the list current.
  • List instances only when ready; deregister and drain before stopping.
  • Discovery can live in the client, a proxy, or a mesh sidecar.
  • An API gateway is the one front door for outside clients.

callout.text: Next up: Sagas — keeping data consistent when one action spans several services.

sagas.title: Sagas & Distributed Transactions
sagas.summary: One action, several services, several databases: how to keep it all-or-nothing without one big transaction.

goals.text: Why one transaction can’t span services
Two-phase commit and why it blocks

steps.title: One trip, three databases
body: A traveller books a trip: a flight, a hotel and a rental car. Each lives in a different service with its own database (database per service, from the previous lessons).
The trip service books the flight — done. The hotel — done. The car — no cars left. Now the traveller has a flight and a hotel they can’t use, and has been charged for both.

callout.text: BEGIN … COMMIT only works inside one database. Across services, there is no built-in “undo everything”.

steps.title: Two-phase commit
body: A classic fix is two-phase commit (2PC). Phase 1: a coordinator asks every participant to prepare — do the work, lock the rows, and promise it can commit (the pings). Phase 2: if all said yes, it tells everyone to commit; if anyone said no, everyone rolls back.
The car service votes no, so nothing is booked anywhere. All or nothing.

callout.text: 2PC is used inside some databases and with XA transactions. It needs every participant to support it — most web APIs and many NoSQL stores don’t.

changes: + Prepare → vote → commit or roll back

tags.text: votes: yes · yes · no → roll back

steps.title: When the coordinator dies
body: The weakness: after preparing, participants must wait for the coordinator’s decision. If it crashes right then, flights and hotels sit “prepared”, holding locks on seats and rooms, unable to commit or roll back on their own.
Other travellers trying to book those seats and rooms wait too — until the coordinator recovers. (The trip itself stays all-or-nothing; it just can’t finish.)

callout.text: 2PC is a blocking protocol: one slow or dead coordinator can freeze every participant. Across services and the internet, that’s usually unacceptable.

steps.title: A saga: commit step by step, undo on failure
body: A saga splits the trip into local transactions that each commit immediately: book flight, then book hotel, then rent car. Nothing is held open.
Every step has a compensating action that semantically undoes it. When the car fails, the saga runs them in reverse: cancel the hotel, then cancel the flight (the red rings).

callout.text: A saga trades isolation for availability: no locks are held across services, but the system is briefly in between states.

steps.title: Orchestration: one service runs the saga
body: In an orchestrated saga, one component — the orchestrator — is a small state machine: it tells each service what to do next, waits for the answer, and decides whether to continue or compensate.
It saves every state change to its own database, so if it crashes it resumes exactly where it stopped.

callout.text: Workflow engines such as Temporal, AWS Step Functions and Camunda are built for this: durable, resumable, observable sagas.

changes: + Saga state saved after every step

steps.title: Choreography: services react to events
body: In a choreographed saga there is no conductor. Flights publishes FlightBooked; Hotels listens, books a room and publishes HotelBooked; Cars listens and rents a car — or publishes CarFailed, which Hotels and Flights react to by cancelling.
No central component to build or run — but the flow is spread across every service, and harder to follow and change.

callout.text: Choreography suits short sagas with few steps. As sagas grow, an orchestrator is usually easier to reason about.

changes: ~ Each service reacts to the previous step’s event

steps.title: The catch: no isolation
body: While a saga runs, other people can see its half-done state: the seat is taken, the hotel isn’t booked yet. And some steps can’t really be undone — an email “your flight is confirmed” has already gone out.
Design for it: use pending states (“reserved”, not “confirmed”), put the step most likely to fail first, and the hardest to undo — charging the card, sending emails — last.

callout.text: A compensation is a new action, not a rollback. A refund is not the same as never having charged.

card.title: Order the steps
lines: 1. check car    likely to fail → first
3. charge card   hard to undo → last

steps.title: Case: crash and resume
body: The orchestrator crashes right after Hotels booked a room — but before it saved that fact. On restart it sees “hotel: pending” and sends the booking request again.
If Hotels books a second room, the traveller pays twice. So every step carries an idempotency key (the saga id + step), and Hotels returns the existing booking instead of creating another.

callout.text: Sagas are at-least-once by nature. Every step and every compensation must be safe to repeat.

steps.title: Case: the undo itself fails
body: The car can’t be rented, so the saga cancels the hotel — but the hotel’s API is down. Giving up isn’t an option: the traveller would be charged for a room they can’t use.
So compensations are retried with backoff until they succeed, and must be safe to repeat. A compensation still stuck after a few hours goes to a queue for a person to resolve.

callout.text: A compensation must be able to succeed eventually. Never design one that can legitimately fail — and alert when one is stuck.

steps.title: Case: a timeout means “unknown”
body: The call to rent the car times out. Did the car service book it before the connection dropped, or not? A timeout is not a failure — the outcome is unknown.

Compensating blindly could cancel a booking that never existed, or leave one that did. Instead, ask: query the car service for request 81-car, or simply retry with the same idempotency key and get the real answer.

callout.text: Treat every remote step as having three outcomes: succeeded, failed, unknown. Only the first two let the saga move on.

steps.title: Recap
body:
• A database transaction can’t span several services.
  • Two-phase commit is all-or-nothing but blocks when the coordinator fails.
  • A saga commits step by step and runs compensations on failure.
  • Orchestrate or choreograph; make every step idempotent.
  • Compensations must eventually succeed; a timeout means unknown, not failed.

callout.text: Next up: Batch & Stream Processing — crunching huge volumes of events, overnight or as they happen.

batch-stream.title: Batch & Stream Processing
batch-stream.summary: Crunching billions of events: overnight in big batches, or continuously as they arrive.

goals.text: Keep analytics off the production database

steps.title: Analytics on the production database
body: Every view of every video is a row in the production database — about 2 billion a day. A dashboard shows views per video, recomputed every minute with a big GROUP BY.
Each run scans the whole day so far — hundreds of millions of rows by mid-morning — and the database that serves the app grinds: viewers wait while it counts.

callout.text: Production databases are tuned for many small, fast queries. Huge scans steal their memory, CPU and disk.

steps.title: Batch: collect now, compute later
body: Instead, the app appends every view as an event to cheap object storage — files, not database rows. Once a night a batch job reads the whole day, computes the counts on a cluster of workers, and writes the results to an analytics warehouse.
The dashboard reads the warehouse. The production database only serves the app again.

callout.text: Batch is simple, cheap and easy to rerun: if the job had a bug, fix it and run it again over the same files.

steps.title: Split the work: map, shuffle, reduce
body: 2 billion events won’t fit through one machine quickly, so the job is split. Map: each worker reads its own chunk of the files and counts views per video. Shuffle: counts for the same video are sent to the same worker. Reduce: that worker adds them up.
Add more workers and the job finishes proportionally faster.

callout.text: This is MapReduce. Today Spark, BigQuery, Snowflake and friends do the same thing behind a SQL interface.

card.title: Counting 2 billion views
lines: map:     each worker counts its chunk
reduce:  sum the counts per video

steps.title: Case: one video, one exhausted reducer
body: One video went viral: 40% of all views yesterday. In the shuffle, every view of it goes to the same reducer. That worker grinds for 3 hours while the other 99 finished in 5 minutes — and the job waits for the slowest.
Splitting work by key only balances it if the keys are balanced. Real data rarely is.

callout.text: Skew is the most common reason a big batch job is mysteriously slow. Look for one task taking far longer than the rest.

steps.title: Combine early, split hot keys
body: Two standard fixes. A combiner pre-aggregates on each mapper: instead of shipping 800 million “view of 4f2” rows, every mapper sends one partial count. For keys that are still too hot, salting splits them — 4f2#0 … 4f2#9 go to ten reducers, and a final step adds the ten totals.
The job drops from 3 hours back to about 20 minutes.

callout.text: Spark and most SQL engines combine automatically for sums and counts, and can detect and split skewed keys for joins.

steps.title: A day late is too late
body: Some questions can’t wait for tonight. A video going viral should show up in “Trending” now. A bot farm faking millions of views should be caught in minutes, before it earns any money.
Running the batch job every hour helps a little, but each run still re-reads a huge pile of data.

callout.text: Batch answers “what happened?”. Some products need “what is happening?”.

changes: − Trending list is a day old

steps.title: Stream processing: compute as events arrive
body: Now the app publishes each view to an event stream (Kafka). A stream processor (Flink, Kafka Streams, Spark Streaming) reads events as they arrive and keeps running counts, writing results to a fast store.
The dashboard is seconds behind reality instead of a day.

callout.text: The processor keeps its counts in local state and checkpoints it regularly, so a crash resumes from the last checkpoint instead of from scratch.

steps.title: Counting in windows
body: A stream never ends, so “count views” needs a time frame: a window. Tumbling windows cut time into fixed slices (views per minute). Sliding windows overlap (views in the last 10 minutes, updated every minute).
A sudden jump between windows is exactly what “trending” — or fraud — looks like.

callout.text: Session windows group events by bursts of activity — useful for “how long did people watch?”.

steps.title: Case: late and duplicate events
body: A phone watches videos in the subway with no signal and uploads its views two hours later. Should they count for 12:04, when they happened, or now, when they arrived? And a flaky network makes some phones send the same event twice.
Stream processors use event time (when it happened), a watermark to decide when a window is complete enough to publish, a policy for stragglers, and an event id to drop duplicates.

callout.text: “Exactly-once” in streaming means checkpoints plus idempotent writes — the same lesson as queues, at billions of events a day.

steps.title: Case: the processor falls behind
body: A celebrity live stream triples traffic for an hour. The stream processor can’t keep up, and unprocessed events pile up in the stream: consumer lag reaches 4 minutes and 18 million events.
Nothing is lost — the stream keeps everything — but the “live” dashboard is now 4 minutes old, and the fraud check runs 4 minutes late.

callout.text: Consumer lag is the key health metric of any streaming system. Alert on it, in seconds or events.

steps.title: Scale out across partitions
body: The stream is split into partitions (by video id, so each video’s events stay in order). Each processor instance owns some partitions, so adding instances adds throughput: two processors, two partitions each.
The backlog drains, lag drops back to seconds, and an autoscaler can add processors whenever lag grows.

callout.text: The number of partitions caps the parallelism. Create more partitions than you need today — adding them later reshuffles keys.

steps.title: Case: counting unique viewers
body: Views are easy to count. Unique viewers are not: to count exactly you must remember every viewer id you’ve seen — 50 million ids for a popular video, about 800 MB of state, per video, per window.
A HyperLogLog sketch estimates the number of distinct ids in 12 KB with about 1% error, and sketches from different machines and windows simply merge.

callout.text: Approximate algorithms (HyperLogLog, count-min sketch, t-digest for percentiles) trade a tiny error for enormous savings. Dashboards rarely need the last 1%.

steps.title: Batch and stream, together
body: Many systems run both: a stream for fast, approximate answers and a nightly batch that recomputes the exact numbers from the full log (the lambda architecture).
Others keep only the stream and, to fix a bug or rebuild results, replay the retained event log through a new version of the processor (the kappa architecture).

BatchStream
FreshnessHoursSeconds
ComplexityLowHigher
RerunEasyReplay the log

callout.text: Start with batch unless you clearly need seconds. Add streaming for the few results that do.

changes: + Nightly batch back alongside the stream

steps.title: Recap
body:
• Keep heavy analytics off the production database.
  • Batch: process large, finished datasets cheaply — results are hours old.
  • Stream: process events as they arrive — seconds old, more moving parts.
  • Watch for skewed keys (combine, salt) and consumer lag (add partitions and processors).
  • Handle late and duplicate events; many systems run both.

callout.text: That completes Architecture. Next module: Security — starting with authentication.

authentication.title: Authentication
authentication.summary: Proving who someone is — without becoming the reason their password leaks.

goals.text: Store passwords as slow, salted hashes
Sessions and a safe password reset

steps.title: A table full of passwords
body: Alice signs up and the login service stores her password exactly as she typed it. Logging in is a simple comparison.

Then a database backup leaks — a misconfigured bucket, a stolen laptop. Every password is readable instantly, and because people reuse passwords, the attacker can now try them on email, banking and everything else.

callout.text: Assume your database will leak one day. The question is what an attacker can do with it.

steps.title: Store a slow, salted hash
body: Never store the password itself. Store a hash: a one-way fingerprint. At login, hash what Alice typed and compare fingerprints.
Use a hash built for passwords — argon2id, bcrypt or scrypt: a random salt per user makes identical passwords look different, and deliberate slowness (~100 ms) turns billions of guesses into years.

callout.text: Fast hashes like MD5 or SHA-256 are the wrong tool: a graphics card tries billions per second.

changes: ~ Passwords → argon2id hashes, salted per user

card.title: Salted, slow hashing
lines: same password, other salt → other hash

steps.title: After login: a session
body: Nobody wants to type a password on every click. After a successful login the service creates a session and gives the browser a random session id in a cookie; later requests present the cookie.
Mark it HttpOnly (scripts can’t read it), Secure (HTTPS only) and SameSite (not sent from other sites). Or issue a short-lived signed token — see the Stateless Services lesson.

callout.text: Treat session ids like passwords: long, random, never in URLs or logs, and invalidated at logout.

steps.title: Case: the forgotten-password flow
body: Password reset is a second way into every account — and often the weakest. Typical bugs: reset tokens that are guessable or never expire, and a form that says “no account with that email”, telling attackers exactly which emails are registered.
A safe flow: a long random token, single use, valid for 15 minutes; the same reply whether or not the account exists; and every existing session signed out after the change.

callout.text: Anything that can change a password — reset, email change, support tools — needs the same care as the login itself.

changes: + Reset email with a single-use token

card.title: A safe reset
lines: same reply whether the email exists
= after the reset: revoke every session

steps.title: Credential stuffing
body: A bot has a list of a billion email + password pairs leaked from other sites. It tries them all against your login form, thousands per second.
Your hashing is perfect — and still about 0.5% of attempts succeed, because those people reused a password. That’s thousands of accounts taken over.

callout.text: Credential stuffing is the most common account-takeover attack. It needs no flaw in your code at all.

steps.title: Make guessing expensive
body: Defend the form itself: rate-limit attempts per account and per IP address, add a challenge when traffic looks automated, and reject passwords that appear in known breach lists at signup.
Flag risky logins — a new device, a new country — and ask for extra proof.

callout.text: Services such as Have I Been Pwned let you check a password against breaches without ever sending the password.

changes: + Rate limits per account and IP

steps.title: A second factor
body: Multi-factor authentication asks for something you have as well as something you know: a code from an authenticator app, a push approval on your phone, or a hardware key.
A stolen password alone no longer opens the account. Passkeys go further: a key pair stored on the device, nothing reusable to steal or phish.

callout.text: SMS codes are better than nothing but can be intercepted (SIM swapping). Prefer app codes, push, or passkeys.

steps.title: Case: a perfect fake login page
body: An email warns of an “unusual sign-in” and links to shop-example.co — a pixel-perfect copy of your login page. Alice types her password and the one-time code from her app.
The fake site relays both to the real one within seconds and walks away with her session. Codes and push approvals stop stolen passwords, but not a phishing site that forwards them in real time.

callout.text: Anything a person can read and type, a fake page can ask for and pass on. Training helps; it isn’t enough on its own.

changes: + Fake login page relaying in real time
− Password and one-time code both captured

steps.title: Passkeys: nothing to type, nothing to steal
body: A passkey (WebAuthn) replaces the password with a key pair kept on Alice’s phone or laptop. To sign in, the device signs a challenge from the site — and the signature is tied to the real domain, shop.example.
On the fake site her device simply has no passkey to offer. There’s nothing to type, nothing to relay, and the server only stores public keys, which are useless to a thief.

callout.text: Passkeys sync across a person’s devices (Apple, Google, password managers), so losing a phone doesn’t lock them out.

steps.title: Or let an identity provider do it
body: “Sign in with Google” uses OpenID Connect (built on OAuth 2.0). Your app sends Alice to the identity provider; she proves who she is there, and the provider sends back a signed ID token saying “this is Alice”.
Your service verifies the signature and never sees, stores or leaks a password. Companies use the same idea for single sign-on (Okta, Entra ID).

callout.text: Authentication is hard to get right. Delegating it to a specialist is often the most secure choice.

steps.title: Case: a stolen token
body: A bug logs request headers, and an attacker finds Alice’s token in the logs. A token is as good as a password while it’s valid — if it never expires, the attacker is Alice forever.
So use short-lived access tokens (minutes) plus a refresh token that is stored carefully and can be revoked. Logging out, or “log out everywhere”, revokes it.

callout.text: Short expiry limits the damage of any leak. Revocation lets you end it immediately.

steps.title: Recap
body:
• Store passwords as slow, salted hashes (argon2id, bcrypt).
  • Sessions in HttpOnly, Secure cookies, or short-lived tokens.
  • Stop stuffing with rate limits, breach checks and a second factor.
  • Make password reset as strong as login; passkeys defeat phishing.
  • Consider an identity provider; keep tokens short-lived and revocable.

callout.text: Next up: Authorization — knowing who someone is doesn’t tell you what they may do.

authorization.title: Authorization
authorization.summary: Knowing who someone is doesn’t tell you what they may see or do. Checking that, everywhere.

steps.title: Logged in is not the same as allowed
body: Eve, from another company, is a legitimate user. She opens her invoice at /invoices/1042, changes the number to 1043 — and sees an invoice belonging to Acme.
The API checked that she was logged in, never that this invoice was hers. This is broken object-level authorization — the most common API security flaw.

callout.text: Hiding a button in the UI is not authorization. Attackers call your API directly, with any id they like.

steps.title: Check ownership on every request
body: Every lookup must be scoped to who is asking: fetch invoice 1043 only if it belongs to the caller’s organisation. For Eve that finds nothing, and she gets 404 Not Found.
Deny by default: any endpoint that forgets the check should fail closed, not open.

callout.text: Answer 404, not 403, for other people’s objects — don’t confirm they exist. Random ids (UUIDs) help, but are no substitute for the check.

changes: + Queries scoped to the caller’s organisation

steps.title: Case: “role”: “admin”
body: Eve edits her own profile — that’s allowed. But the API takes the JSON body and saves every field in it. So she adds "role": "admin" to the request and promotes herself.
This is mass assignment. Fix: each endpoint has an allow-list of fields it may change, and roles change only through a separate admin-only endpoint.

callout.text: Frameworks that bind request bodies straight onto database models make this easy to get wrong. Be explicit about writable fields.

changes: − API saves it · Eve is admin

steps.title: Let the database enforce tenants too
body: Ownership checks live in application code, so one query that forgets AND org_id = … brings the leak right back. Add a second layer: row-level security in the database.
The app tells each connection which organisation it is serving; the database then filters every query by that org. Even SELECT * FROM invoices only returns the caller’s rows.

callout.text: Defence in depth: assume any single check will eventually be forgotten, and make sure a second one is there.

changes: ~ App sets the caller’s org per connection

steps.title: Roles: what each kind of user may do
body: Inside Acme, people need different powers: some only view invoices, some edit them, a few approve large ones. Rather than list permissions per person, group them into roles and give each person a role — role-based access control (RBAC).
Alice is an accountant: she can edit invoices but not approve them.

callout.text: Keep roles few and meaningful. Hundreds of special-case roles become impossible to reason about.

steps.title: Relationships: sharing and teams
body: Roles struggle with sharing: “Alice can see this folder because it was shared with her team”. Relationship-based access (ReBAC) stores facts like “invoice 1042 is in folder Q3”, “Q3 is shared with team Finance”, “Alice is in Finance”, and follows the chain.
This is how Google Docs-style sharing works at scale.

callout.text: Google’s Zanzibar paper popularised this model; SpiceDB and OpenFGA are open-source versions.

steps.title: Decide in one place
body: Permission checks scattered as if-statements across twenty services drift apart, and nobody can answer “who can approve invoices?”. Instead, each service asks a policy service: “may Alice edit invoice 1042?”, and enforces the yes or no.
The rules live in one place, are tested like code, and every decision can be logged.

callout.text: Tools: Open Policy Agent (Rego), AWS Cedar, or a permissions service like SpiceDB. Cache decisions briefly to keep calls fast.

steps.title: Case: a service with keys to everything
body: The reports service connects to the database with the admin account — it was quickest to set up. One day a SQL-injection bug is found in a report filter.
Because the service could read every table, the attacker dumps users, password hashes and payment details too — not just invoices.

callout.text: A component’s permissions define the blast radius of its bugs.

changes: + Reports service with admin DB credentials

steps.title: Least privilege
body: Give every service — and every person — only the access its job needs. The reports service gets a read-only account that can see the invoices view and nothing else; each service has its own credentials and identity.
The same injection bug now leaks, at worst, invoices the service could already read — and alarms fire when it tries anything else.

callout.text: Apply it everywhere: database grants, cloud IAM roles, API scopes, and staff access (time-limited, approved, logged).

steps.title: Case: the confused deputy
body: Alice asks for a report of invoices over $10,000. The API hands the job to the reports service, which queries with its own identity — and it may read every tenant’s invoices. Alice’s report includes Globex’s.
The reports service was tricked into using its authority on someone else’s behalf: a confused deputy.

callout.text: Whenever a service acts for a user, ask: whose permissions apply here — the service’s or the user’s?

changes: + Report runs as the reports service

steps.title: Act as the user, not as yourself
body: Pass the user’s identity along: the API forwards Alice’s token (or exchanges it for a narrower one), and the reports service runs the query as Alice — with her organisation and her permissions.
The service’s own powerful credentials are only used for things no user asked for, like nightly maintenance.

callout.text: OAuth token exchange and service meshes can carry the end user’s identity across every hop automatically.

steps.title: Audit logs: who saw what
body: Finally, record every access to sensitive data — who, what, when, from where — in an append-only audit log that the people being audited can’t edit.
It answers “who looked at this customer’s invoices?” after an incident, and powers alerts: a support agent opening 5,000 invoices in ten minutes is worth a page.

callout.text: Audit logs are also required by most compliance standards (SOC 2, HIPAA, GDPR requests).

steps.title: Recap
body:
• Check that the caller may access this object, on every request.
  • Use roles for kinds of users, relationships for sharing.
  • Decide in a central policy; enforce in each service.
  • Allow-list writable fields; add row-level security as a second layer.
  • Grant least privilege; act as the user, not as the service; keep an audit log.

callout.text: Next up: Encryption & Secrets — protecting data on the wire, on disk, and the keys themselves.

encryption.title: Encryption & Secrets
encryption.summary: Protecting data on the wire, on disk, and the keys and passwords your services use.

goals.text: Encryption inside the data center and at rest

steps.title: Plain HTTP on café Wi-Fi
body: Alice logs in from a café. The site uses plain http://, so her password and session cookie travel as readable text through the Wi-Fi router and a dozen networks beyond it.
Mallory, on the same Wi-Fi, records the traffic and reads everything — and could even change pages on the way back.

callout.text: Anyone on the path — Wi-Fi, ISP, a compromised router — can read and alter unencrypted traffic.

steps.title: TLS: encrypt the wire
body: With HTTPS, TLS encrypts everything between Alice’s browser and the site. During the handshake the server presents a certificate, signed by a certificate authority the browser trusts, proving it really is shop.example.
Mallory still copies every packet — but sees only random-looking bytes, and can’t alter them without detection.

callout.text: Certificates are free and automatic with Let’s Encrypt. Add HSTS so browsers never fall back to http://.

changes: + TLS certificate on the load balancer

card.title: The TLS handshake
lines: both agree on fresh session keys

steps.title: Case: the certificate expired at 3 a.m.
body: Certificates have an expiry date. This one was renewed by hand once a year — by someone who has since left. At 03:00 it expires, every browser shows a full-page security warning, and most users leave.
An outage caused by a date. Fix: automatic renewal with ACME (Let’s Encrypt, or your cloud’s certificate manager), and an alert 30 days before any certificate expires.

callout.text: Short-lived certificates (90 days or less) force automation — and limit the damage if a private key ever leaks.

card.title: Never expire by surprise
lines: ! renewed by hand, once a year
# check every endpoint, not just www

steps.title: Encrypt inside the data center too
body: The load balancer terminates TLS — and traditionally sent plain traffic onward, trusting the internal network. But one compromised machine inside could then read everything.
Modern systems assume no network is trusted (zero trust): services talk over mutual TLS, where both sides present certificates, so every hop is encrypted and every caller is identified.

callout.text: A service mesh can add mTLS between all services automatically, with short-lived certificates it rotates for you.

changes: ~ LB → app → DB over mutual TLS
+ Every service has its own certificate

steps.title: The stolen backup
body: Every byte on the wire is now safe. Then a database backup is left in a storage bucket that was accidentally made public, and someone copies it.
Encryption in transit does nothing here: the data on disk — every customer’s name, address and order history — is readable.

callout.text: Disks get lost, snapshots get shared, buckets get misconfigured. Data at rest needs its own protection.

steps.title: Encrypt at rest, keep keys elsewhere
body: Encrypt disks, database files and backups. The trick is the key: if it sits next to the data, a thief takes both. So keys live in a separate key management service (KMS), which never hands out its master key.
With envelope encryption, data is encrypted with a data key, and the data key is itself encrypted by the KMS. Every use of a key is logged, and access can be revoked.

callout.text: Cloud databases and storage encrypt at rest with a checkbox. For very sensitive fields, also encrypt in the application.

card.title: Envelope encryption
lines: data key —encrypted by→ KMS master key
= steal the disk: no usable key

steps.title: Rotating keys without re-encrypting everything
body: Keys should change regularly — and immediately if one might have leaked. Re-encrypting terabytes of data would take days.
Envelope encryption makes it cheap: create a new master key in the KMS and re-wrap each small data key with it. The data itself is never touched, and new writes simply get fresh data keys.

callout.text: Most KMSs rotate master keys automatically every year and keep old versions to unwrap older data keys.

changes: + Master key v2 in the KMS

card.title: Rotating keys
lines: new master key v2 in the KMS
# new writes use fresh data keys

steps.title: Case: a secret in the code
body: A developer hard-codes the payment provider’s API key in the source to test something, and the repository is public. Bots scan public repositories continuously: the key is found and used within minutes.
Deleting the line doesn’t help — it’s in the git history forever. The only fix is to revoke the key and issue a new one.

callout.text: Secrets in code end up in repos, builds, logs and laptops. Treat any secret that touched git as compromised.

changes: + API key committed to a public repo
− Found by a scanner bot in minutes

steps.title: A secrets manager
body: Keep secrets out of code entirely. The app fetches them at startup from a secrets manager (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager), proving its own identity to get only the secrets it needs.
Secrets are rotated regularly — or issued short-lived on demand — and scanners in CI block any commit that looks like a key.

callout.text: Never log secrets, and keep them out of error messages and environment dumps.

changes: + Automatic rotation · secret scanning in CI

steps.title: Case: card numbers — tokenize them
body: Card numbers are the most valuable data you could hold, and every system that stores or even sees them must meet strict rules (PCI DSS). Encrypting them still leaves you holding them.

Better: don’t hold them. The checkout sends the card to a payment provider, which stores it and returns a token like tok_4f2c. Your database, logs and analytics only ever see tokens — worthless to a thief.

callout.text: The safest sensitive data is data you never store. Ask whether you need it at all before deciding how to protect it.

changes: + Payment provider holds the real card numbers

steps.title: End-to-end: even the server can’t read it
body: For private messages you can go further. With end-to-end encryption, Alice’s phone encrypts each message with Bob’s public key; only Bob’s phone holds the private key to decrypt it.
The chat server stores and forwards ciphertext. A breach of the server — or a request to hand over messages — reveals nothing readable.
That’s the idea in one line. Real protocols use the key pairs to agree on a fresh secret key for every message, so a key stolen later can’t unlock old conversations (forward secrecy).

callout.text: The trade-off: the server can’t search, filter or back up readable messages, and losing your device can mean losing history. Signal and WhatsApp use the Signal protocol.

steps.title: Recap
body:
• TLS everywhere outside; mTLS between services inside.
  • Encrypt at rest, with keys held separately in a KMS.
  • Automate certificate renewal; rotate keys by re-wrapping data keys.
  • Keep secrets in a secrets manager, rotate them, scan for leaks.
  • Tokenize what you’d rather not hold at all, like card numbers.
  • End-to-end encryption when even the server shouldn’t read the data.

callout.text: That completes Security. Next module: Shipping — testing changes and getting them to production safely.

testing.title: Testing
testing.summary: Knowing a change is safe before your users find out — fast tests for the logic, a few slow ones for everything else.

goals.text: End-to-end tests and the test pyramid
Flaky tests, and testing for load and failure

steps.title: Is this change safe?
body: The checkout service applies discount codes. It reads and writes the orders database, charges cards through an external payment provider, and asks the Inventory team’s service whether items are in stock.
A developer has just changed how discounts are rounded. Before shipping, the team checks it by hand: click through a few purchases on a test server, and it all looks fine.

callout.text: Every change carries a question: what else did this break? Tests are how you answer it quickly, every time, without relying on anyone remembering what to check.

steps.title: Clicking around misses things
body: Nobody tried a basket of three items at €9.99 with a 10% code. The new rounding charges €26.98 instead of €26.97 — a cent too much on thousands of orders before support notices.
Manual checks are slow, so they happen rarely, and they only cover what someone thought to try. The bug was found by users.

callout.text: The later a bug is found, the more it costs: seconds in a test, hours in review, days in production — plus refunds and trust.

changes: − Found by customers, not by the team

steps.title: Unit tests: one piece, in isolation
body: A unit test calls one function with known inputs and checks the output — here, the total for a given basket and code. It runs in milliseconds, with no database and no network.
Because they’re so cheap, you write thousands, and they run on every change. The rounding case becomes one line that fails the moment someone breaks it again.

callout.text: Write the test for a bug before you fix it: watch it fail, fix the code, watch it pass. That bug can never quietly come back.

steps.title: Test doubles stand in for the rest
body: Checkout can’t run without its dependencies, so tests swap them for test doubles: a fake database that lives in memory, a stub provider that always answers “approved”, a mock that records whether a card was charged exactly once.
The catch: a double only knows what you told it. If the real provider renames a field, every unit test still passes.

callout.text: Doubles make tests fast and repeatable, and they can quietly drift from reality. Something has to test against the real thing too.

changes: + Fake database, stub provider, stub Inventory

steps.title: Integration tests: the real neighbours
body: An integration test runs Checkout against a real database — started fresh in a container for the test run — and checks what actually lands in the tables. SQL typos, broken migrations and mismatched types show up here, not in production.
The payment provider stays stubbed (you can’t charge real cards), but you can call its sandbox in a separate, smaller suite.

callout.text: Containers made this cheap: a throwaway PostgreSQL or Kafka takes seconds to start, so integration tests can run on every change too.

changes: ~ Fake database → real database in a container

db.label: orders db · real, in a container

steps.title: Contract tests: between teams
body: Checkout depends on Inventory, which another team owns and deploys on its own schedule. If they rename in_stock to available, Checkout’s stub never notices.

A contract test writes down what Checkout expects — this request, a response with these fields — and Inventory’s own pipeline checks every change against it. A breaking change fails in their build, before it ships.

callout.text: Tools like Pact record these consumer expectations. Contracts replace most of the slow end-to-end tests that would otherwise be needed between services.

changes: + Checkout’s expectations recorded as a contract
+ Inventory verifies it on every change

db.label: orders db · real, in a container

card.title: The contract
lines: # checked on both sides, run separately

steps.title: End-to-end tests: the whole journey
body: An end-to-end test drives the real system the way a user would: open the shop in a browser, add three items, enter a code, pay with a sandbox card, see the confirmation.
It is the only test that proves everything works together — and the slowest, most fragile one. A dozen of them for the journeys that make money is plenty.

callout.text: An end-to-end test tells you something broke, not what. When one fails, the cheaper tests below it should point to the cause.

changes: + A browser test drives the whole system

steps.title: The test pyramid
body: Put together, the suites form a test pyramid: thousands of unit tests at the bottom, hundreds of integration and contract tests in the middle, a handful of end-to-end tests on top.
Lower layers are fast, precise and cheap to run on every change; higher ones are slow but closer to what users do. Push each check as low as it can go.

callout.text: An upside-down pyramid — mostly end-to-end tests — is a common trap: an hour per run, frequent random failures, and a team that stops trusting red builds.

card.title: Three layers
lines: = unit         2,000    30 s    one piece at a time
# fast and many at the bottom, few at the top

steps.title: Case: the flaky test
body: One end-to-end test fails about one run in twenty. It waits a fixed two seconds for the confirmation email, and sometimes the email takes three. People learn to press “re-run” — and when a real bug turns that test red, they re-run that too.
A flaky test is worse than no test: it trains the team to ignore failures.

callout.text: Fix the cause: wait for a condition instead of a fixed time, control the clock, give each test its own data, never depend on test order. Track flaky tests and fix or delete them — don’t hide them behind automatic retries.

changes: − Fails 1 run in 20 for no reason
− Real failures get re-run and ignored

steps.title: Testing for load and for failure
body: Correct isn’t enough. A load test sends production-like traffic to a copy of the system and finds the point where latency turns upward (see Latency & Throughput) before your users do.
Failure tests break things on purpose — stop a database replica, slow the payment provider down — and check that timeouts, retries and failover behave as designed (see Timeouts & Retries).

callout.text: The last layer runs in production itself: release to a few users first and watch the numbers. That is the canary in the next lesson.

changes: + Load test: 5× normal traffic on staging
+ Failure test: payment provider slowed to 5 s

steps.title: Recap
body:
• Unit tests check one piece with doubles for the rest — fast enough to run thousands on every change.
  • Integration tests use real neighbours (a database in a container) to catch what doubles can’t.
  • Contract tests catch breaking API changes between teams, in the provider’s own build.
  • A few end-to-end tests cover the journeys that matter: keep the pyramid the right way up.
  • Fix flaky tests, and test for load and failure, not just correctness.

callout.text: Next up: CI/CD & Deployments — running all of this on every change, and getting it to production safely.

cicd.title: CI/CD & Deployments
cicd.summary: Getting every change to production quickly and safely — and back out again just as quickly.

goals.text: Migrations that don’t break the old version

steps.title: Shipping by hand
body: Once a week, on Friday evening, a developer builds the app on their laptop, copies it to the production server over SSH and restarts it. Everyone stays late in case something breaks.
A week of everyone’s changes goes out at once — so when something does break, nobody is sure which change did it.

callout.text: Big, rare releases feel safer and are the opposite: the more that changes at once, the harder it is to test, to find the cause, and to undo.

steps.title: “It works on my machine”
body: This Friday the laptop had a newer library than the server, and the app won’t start. While the developer works out which of thirty changes to undo, the site is down.
There is no record of exactly what was running before, so even going back is guesswork. Four hours later, it’s up again.

callout.text: Builds that depend on someone’s machine, and deploys nobody can repeat exactly, turn every release into an experiment.

steps.title: Continuous integration
body: Now every push to the shared repository starts a pipeline on a clean machine: build the code, run the tests (see Testing). Nothing depends on anyone’s laptop.
The team merges small changes into main several times a day. A red pipeline means “stop and fix this first”, so main always builds and passes. That habit is continuous integration.

callout.text: Keep the pipeline fast — ten minutes, not an hour. A slow pipeline makes people batch their changes again.

changes: + Shared repository, small changes to main
+ Every push: build + test on a clean machine

steps.title: Build once, promote the same artifact
body: The last stage packages the result into an immutable artifact — usually a container image — tagged with the commit it came from, checkout:3f9c2a1, and stores it in a registry.
That exact image is what gets tested, deployed to staging and then to production. Only configuration (addresses, secrets) differs between environments. What you tested is what you ship.

callout.text: Never rebuild for production: a rebuild can pull different dependencies and produce a different program from the one you tested.

changes: + Package stage: one image per commit

steps.title: Continuous delivery
body: Every image that passes is deployed to staging automatically — a small copy of production — where smoke tests check the main journeys. From there it can go to production at any time.
With continuous delivery, production is one button press away. With continuous deployment, there is no button: every green change goes out by itself.

callout.text: Deploying daily makes each deploy small: a few changes, easy to review, easy to blame, easy to undo.

steps.title: Blue-green: switch, don’t replace
body: How does a new version reach users without downtime? With blue-green deployment there are two identical production groups. Blue serves everyone on v41 while v42 starts on green and warms up.
Then the load balancer switches all traffic to green at once. If anything looks wrong, switching back to blue takes seconds — it is still running, untouched.

callout.text: The cost is double capacity during a release. Rolling deploys (see Load Balancing) are cheaper but slower to undo.

changes: + Two production groups: blue (v41) and green (v42)
~ Load balancer switches all traffic to green

steps.title: Canary: try it on a few users first
body: A canary release sends a small slice of real traffic — here 5% — to the new version, and compares its error rate and latency with the old version’s (see Observability).
If v42 is worse, the pipeline rolls it back automatically and only a few users ever saw it. If it holds up, the slice grows: 25%, 50%, everyone.

callout.text: Canaries are testing in production — the only environment with real users, real data and real traffic patterns.

steps.title: Case: the migration that breaks the old version
body: v42 renames a column: name becomes full_name. The migration runs, and v42 is happy — but during the rollout most servers are still on v41, which asks for name and gets an error.
Fix it with expand and contract: add full_name and write both; backfill old rows; switch reads to full_name; only when no running version uses name, drop it. Every step works with both versions.

callout.text: During any deploy, old and new code run side by side against the same database. Every schema change must work with both.

changes: + Expand → migrate → contract, over several deploys

card.title: Expand, then contract
lines: = 4  drop name — once nothing uses it

steps.title: Feature flags: deploy is not release
body: The new checkout page is merged and deployed weeks before launch — switched off. A feature flag decides, per request, who sees it: first the team, then 1% of users, then everyone.
Turning it off is a setting, not a deploy, so a problem is fixed in seconds. Deploying (moving code to servers) and releasing (showing it to users) become separate decisions.

callout.text: Flags are debt too: remove each one once its feature is fully out, or the code fills with branches nobody dares delete.

changes: ~ New checkout: on for staff + 1% of users

steps.title: Measure the delivery itself
body: Four numbers, known as the DORA metrics, describe how well a team ships: how often it deploys, how long a change takes from commit to production, how many deploys cause a problem, and how quickly service is restored when one does.
Research across thousands of teams found the same thing this lesson shows: the teams that ship most often also break production least, because every change is small and every undo is fast.

callout.text: Speed and safety are not a trade-off here. Small, frequent, reversible changes improve both.

steps.title: Recap
body:
• CI: small changes merged often; every push is built and tested on a clean machine.
  • Build once: one immutable artifact per commit, promoted unchanged to every environment.
  • CD: every green change can reach production at any time — by a click or automatically.
  • Release carefully: blue-green to switch back fast, canaries to limit the damage, flags to separate deploy from release.
  • Schema changes must work with old and new code at once: expand, then contract.

callout.text: That completes Shipping. Next module: Whole Systems — starting with how high-level and low-level design fit together.

hld-lld.title: HLD & LLD
hld-lld.summary: The same system at two zoom levels: the map of services, and the inside of one of them.

goals.text: How a design session moves between them

steps.title: One system, two zoom levels
body: A food-delivery app. From far away it is a handful of services — Orders, Couriers, Payments — each with its own data, talking through an API gateway and a stream of events.
Up close, each of those boxes is a program of its own, with classes, tables and rules. System design works at both distances, and they have names: high-level design (HLD) and low-level design (LLD).

callout.text: Neither is “more real”. They answer different questions, for different readers, and change at different speeds.

steps.title: High-level design: the map
body: HLD decides what the parts are and how they connect: which services exist and what each owns, how they talk (a call, or an event), where each kind of data lives, and what happens when traffic grows or a part fails.
It is the level of every lesson so far. Its output is a diagram like this one, with the reasoning written next to it.

callout.text: A good HLD fits on one page. If a box needs a paragraph to explain, that paragraph belongs to the LLD of that box.

changes: + The whole system is the unit of design

card.title: HLD decides
lines: which services exist, what each owns
how it scales, how it fails

steps.title: HLD decisions are trade-offs
body: Placing an order should not wait for a courier to be found, so Orders publishes an event and Couriers picks it up when it can (see Pub/Sub & Events).

Payments needs transactions, so it gets a relational database. Couriers send their location every few seconds — tens of thousands of writes a second, each overwriting the last — so that store is a fast key–value one. Each choice comes from the numbers and from what the data needs.

callout.text: Every arrow and every store on an HLD diagram is a decision with an alternative. Be ready to say what you gave up.

changes: ~ Orders → Couriers: an event, not a call

card.title: Decisions at this level
lines: Orders → Couriers   an event, not a call
# each one has an alternative you gave up

steps.title: Low-level design: inside one box
body: Now open the Orders box. LLD decides how one component is built: the modules or classes it is made of, the interfaces between them, its tables and indexes, its algorithms and its error handling.
Here a controller takes HTTP requests, an order service holds the rules, a repository talks to the database, and a client wraps the calls to Payments.

callout.text: Keeping the database and other services behind small interfaces (the yellow parts) is what makes the core logic easy to test — see Testing.

changes: + Inside Orders: controller, service, repository, payment client

steps.title: LLD decisions: states, schemas, edge cases
body: An order moves through states, and LLD pins down which moves are allowed: it can be cancelled while placed or paid, but not once the kitchen has started.
It also settles the table (columns, types, an index on (user_id, created_at) for “my orders”) and the awkward cases: what if the payment call times out, or the same order arrives twice?

callout.text: Most production bugs live at this level: a state change nobody allowed for, a missing index, a retry that charges twice.

card.title: Order states
lines: placed → paid → cooking → on the way → delivered
= cancel: only from placed or paid

steps.title: Where they meet: contracts
body: The two levels meet at the edges of each box. HLD fixes what a component promises — its API and the events it publishes. LLD decides how it keeps that promise.
That split is what lets teams work independently: Orders can rewrite everything inside its box, as long as POST /orders and OrderPlaced keep meaning the same thing.

callout.text: Changing a contract is an HLD change: other teams must agree, and old and new versions must work side by side for a while (see REST, RPC & GraphQL on versioning).

changes: + The contract at the edge of the service

steps.title: Case: designing at the wrong level
body: Asked to design this app in an interview, one candidate spends twenty minutes on class diagrams and never mentions that courier locations arrive 40,000 times a second. Another draws perfect boxes, but can’t say how an order avoids being charged twice.
Work top-down: requirements, rough numbers, the HLD — then dive into the one or two places where the hard problems are, and do those at the LLD level.

callout.text: A design session usually runs: requirements → estimates → API → data model → HLD → deep dives → failure cases. The walkthroughs that follow use exactly this order.

changes: + Deep dives: location writes, double charges

metrics.unit: the whole, then the risky parts
