body:
HLDLLD
ZoomWhole systemOne component
PartsServices, stores, queuesClasses, tables, states
DecidesWhat talks to what, where data livesHow each part works inside
ChangesRarely, with agreementOften, within a team
This course works at the HLD level and dips into LLD where a decision depends on it. LLD — object-oriented design, design patterns — is a subject of its own.

callout.text: Next up: Design a URL Shortener — the first full walkthrough, from a one-line brief to a finished design.

design-url-shortener.title: Design a URL Shortener
design-url-shortener.summary: A first end-to-end design: from a one-line brief to a system that serves billions of redirects.

goals.text: Turn a brief into requirements and numbers
Generate short codes that never collide
Design the read path: cache and redirect type
Store billions of key → value rows
Keep analytics and abuse off the critical path

steps.title: The brief: a link shortener
body: Time to use everything at once, top-down as in HLD & LLD. The task: build a service like bit.ly. Paste a long URL, get a short one back — sho.rt/x7Kp2Qa — and anyone who opens it is redirected to the original.

Before drawing boxes, pin down what “works” means. It must: create a short link, and redirect. It should: expire links and count clicks. And the qualities that matter: redirects have to be fast and almost never fail — a dead shortener breaks every link ever shared — while creating a link may take a moment longer.

callout.text: Every design starts with the same three questions: what must it do, how much of it, and what matters most when you can’t have everything?

card.title: Requirements
lines: # creating a link may be slower

steps.title: Put numbers on it
body: Napkin math first (Module 01). Say 100 million new links a month — about 40 writes a second. Each link is opened roughly 100 times, so redirects average 4,000 a second and peak near 12,000.
Kept for five years, that’s 6 billion links. At about 500 bytes each: 3 TB. Two things jump out: the system is read-heavy — a hundred reads for every write — and the data is large but very simple.

callout.text: The numbers choose the design. “100 reads per write” says cache. “3 TB of key → value rows” says this will have to spread across machines.

steps.title: The simplest thing that works
body: Two endpoints. POST /links stores a URL and returns a code; GET /x7Kp2Qa looks the code up and answers with a redirect.
One table does it: code (the primary key), long_url, created_at, expires_at. Stateless API servers behind a load balancer, plus one database, make a perfectly good version one.

callout.text: Start with the simplest design that meets the brief, then ask what breaks first. Two questions are still open: where do the codes come from, and what happens at 12,000 reads a second?

steps.title: Where do codes come from? Try a hash
body: First idea: hash the long URL and keep the first seven characters. No coordination needed, and the same URL always gives the same code.

But seven characters can’t hold a whole hash, so different URLs will sometimes collide — and with billions of links, constantly. Every insert has to check “is this code already taken by another URL?” and retry with a tweak. Worse, two users shortening the same URL get the same code, so neither can have their own expiry or statistics.

callout.text: Truncated hashes collide far sooner than intuition says — the birthday problem. With 3.5 trillion possible codes, expect the first clash after only about two million links.

changes: − Collisions: check and retry on every insert

card.title: Two URLs, one code
lines: # check, tweak, retry — on every write

steps.title: Count, then encode
body: Better: give every link a unique number and write that number in base 62 — digits, lowercase and uppercase letters. A unique number in means a unique code out, with nothing to check.

Seven base-62 characters cover 62⁷ ≈ 3.5 trillion links, hundreds of times more than we need. The numbers come straight from Unique IDs at Scale: each API server reserves a block of a million ids from a small counter service, then counts through it locally.

callout.text: Encoding is repeated division: 125 ÷ 62 = 2 remainder 1, so 125 becomes “21”. Decoding reverses it — the code is the id.

changes: + Counter service handing out blocks of ids
~ Code = the id written in base 62

steps.title: Case: codes you can count
body: Counter codes come out in order: tn1e, tn1f, tn1g. Anyone can walk the whole space and harvest every link ever made — including the “private” document links and password-reset URLs people shortened.

The fix keeps the uniqueness and loses the order. Either scramble each id with a reversible shuffle (a keyed permutation) before encoding it, or pick seven random characters and let the table’s unique key reject the rare duplicate.

callout.text: Unguessable codes slow scraping down. They are not security: anything truly private needs real access control (Module 07).

changes: ~ Codes look random and still never collide

steps.title: Reads dominate: cache them
body: Now the read path. A small share of links gets most of the clicks — today’s viral post, not last year’s — and a link never changes once it’s created. That is the ideal case for a cache (see Caching).

Put an in-memory cache in front, mapping code → long_url. About 90% of redirects stop there within a millisecond; the database only sees the misses. Since links are immutable there is almost nothing to invalidate: a TTL and LRU eviction are enough.

callout.text: Don’t forget negative caching. Bots request random codes all day; cache “no such code” too, or every one of them becomes a database lookup.

changes: ~ 90% of redirects never reach the database

steps.title: Which redirect: 301 or 302?
body: 301 Moved Permanently lets the browser remember the answer, so the next click never reaches you. It’s the cheapest request there is — and it means you can no longer count that click, change the destination, or expire the link for that user.
302 Found is temporary: every click comes back to you. More load, but you keep control and analytics. Most shorteners choose 302 and let the cache absorb the cost.

callout.text: A whole design decision hiding in a status code: who gets to cache the answer, and for how long?

changes: ~ Decision: answer with 302 — keep analytics and control

card.title: Two kinds of redirect
lines: ! no click counts, edits or expiry

steps.title: Three terabytes of keys: spread them out
body: Six billion rows won’t stay comfortable on one machine. But look at how the data is used: every query is “get this one code”. No joins, no range scans, no multi-row transactions.

That is exactly what a key–value store is for — DynamoDB, Cassandra (see SQL vs NoSQL). Partition by a hash of the code so load spreads evenly (Sharding, Consistent Hashing), and keep three copies of every partition in different zones (Replication).

callout.text: Because the codes look random, hashing them balances almost perfectly — no hot partition. Partitioning by creation date would have sent nearly all traffic to “today”.

changes: ~ One database → key–value store (3 partitions shown)
+ 3 replicas of each partition, across zones
~ Every redirect touches exactly one partition

steps.title: Counting clicks without slowing them
body: Product wants click counts per link. The naive way — UPDATE links SET clicks = clicks + 1 on every redirect — turns 4,000 cheap reads a second into 4,000 writes, all landing on the hottest rows.

Instead, the API server drops a tiny click event onto a stream and answers the redirect straight away. A consumer adds the events up into per-link counts every few seconds (see Message Queues and Batch & Stream Processing).

callout.text: The redirect is the product; the count is a by-product. Never put the by-product on the critical path.

changes: + A stream job aggregates the counts
~ Redirect path unchanged: still about 5 ms

steps.title: Case: spammers love shorteners
body: A short link hides where it goes — ideal for phishing. A script starts creating 5,000 links a minute that point at fake bank pages. Soon your whole domain is on blocklists, and every customer’s links stop working.

Defend in layers. Rate-limit link creation per account and per IP (Rate Limiting). Check every destination against phishing and malware lists, when it’s created and again later. And let links expire, so abandoned ones stop being a liability.

callout.text: Operations are part of the design. For most link shorteners the first serious incident isn’t load — it’s abuse.

steps.title: The finished design
body:
QuestionDecisionBecause
CodesScrambled counter, base 62Unique with no checks
Read pathCache + 302100 reads per write
StorageKey–value, hash-partitionedOne-key lookups, 3 TB
ClicksEvents on a streamOff the critical path
AbuseLimits, checks, expiryProtect the domain
Notice the method more than the answer: requirements → numbers → simplest design → find the bottleneck → fix it → repeat.

callout.text: Next up: Design a News Feed — where the hard part isn’t storing posts, but deciding when to do the work.

design-news-feed.title: Design a News Feed
design-news-feed.summary: Posts from everyone you follow, in 200 ms — and the question of when to do the work.

goals.text: Size the read and write load of a feed
Fan-out on read vs fan-out on write
Why celebrities break pure push — and the hybrid fix
What to store, and for whom

steps.title: The brief: a home feed
body: Second design. A social app: people follow each other, and the home screen shows recent posts from everyone you follow, newest first.

What matters: opening the feed must feel instant — under 200 ms. A new post should reach followers within a few seconds, but not necessarily at the same instant for everyone. Eventual consistency is fine: nobody is harmed if a post shows up five seconds late.

callout.text: Notice the freedom in that last requirement. Deciding what does not have to be immediate or exact is what makes large systems possible.

card.title: Requirements
lines: home feed   posts from people I follow
# a new post may take a few seconds

steps.title: Put numbers on it
body: 200 million people use it daily and open the feed about ten times each: 2 billion feed loads a day, or 23,000 a second on average. They write 50 million posts a day — about 600 a second.
So feeds are read roughly 40 times more often than posts are written. And a typical user follows 200 accounts. Remember that number.

callout.text: Two numbers will drive everything that follows: reads outnumber writes 40 to 1, and every feed draws on 200 sources.

card.title: Napkin math
lines: = about 40 feed reads per post written

steps.title: First draft: build the feed when it’s asked for
body: Store posts in a table indexed by (author_id, created_at), sharded by author. To build Alice’s feed: find the 200 accounts she follows, fetch the latest posts of each, merge them by time, return the top 20.
This is the pull model, or fan-out on read. Posting is as cheap as it gets — one insert — and a new post is visible to everyone at once.

callout.text: Nothing is precomputed, so nothing can go stale and nothing needs repairing. For a small app, this is the right design.

changes: + Feed = query 200 authors, merge, keep the top 20

steps.title: The work lands on the wrong side
body: Every feed load fans out to 200 authors spread over many shards, and has to wait for the slowest answer — the fan-out tail from Latency & Throughput.

Worse is the total: 23,000 feed loads a second × 200 lookups = 4.6 million lookups a second, mostly recomputing a result identical to what the same person saw a minute ago. The expensive work sits on the path that runs 40 times more often.

callout.text: When reads far outnumber writes, move the work to write time.

card.title: Cost of pull
lines: # and each load waits for the slowest shard

steps.title: Flip it: deliver posts when they’re written
body: Give every user a ready-made feed: a list in a cache, newest first. When Ana posts, a fan-out worker looks up her followers and adds the post to each of their lists. This is the push model, or fan-out on write.
Opening the feed is now one read of one list. The fan-out runs behind a queue (Message Queues), so Ana’s post returns immediately and her followers see it a second or two later.

callout.text: The arithmetic works: 600 posts/s × 200 followers ≈ 120,000 small cache writes a second — far cheaper than 4.6 million lookups.

changes: + Feed cache: one list per user

steps.title: Store ids, not posts
body: Each feed list holds only post ids — a few bytes apiece — and only the newest 800 or so. When a feed is read, the API fetches the posts themselves in one batch from the post store (“hydration”).
Keeping a single copy of every post means an edit or a delete happens in one place. A deleted post is simply dropped during hydration; nobody has to chase it through millions of lists.

callout.text: 200 million lists × 800 ids × 8 bytes ≈ 1.3 TB of memory: a big cache cluster, but an ordinary one. Storing whole posts would cost a hundred times as much.

changes: ~ Feed lists hold post ids only, capped at 800
+ Posts fetched in one batch at read time
~ Edits and deletes happen in one place

steps.title: Case: fifty million followers
body: A pop star with 50 million followers posts. That single post becomes 50 million cache writes. Even at 100,000 writes a second, delivery takes more than eight minutes — and the queue is so backed up that everyone else’s posts wait behind it.
It’s the hot-key problem from Sharding: one unusually heavy key overwhelms a design tuned for the average.

callout.text: Averages hide this. The typical account has 200 followers; a few thousand accounts have millions — and they post at the busiest moments.

changes: + A celebrity posts to 50 M followers
− 50 M feed writes for one post

steps.title: Hybrid: push for most, pull for the famous
body: Treat the two kinds of account differently. Ordinary users keep fan-out on write. Accounts above a threshold — say 100,000 followers — are not fanned out at all.

When Alice opens her feed, the API reads her ready-made list and pulls the latest posts of the handful of celebrities she follows — each one a single cached timeline — then merges the two. A few extra lookups per read, instead of 50 million writes per post.

callout.text: Neither pure strategy survives real data. Large designs usually end up as a hybrid, split along exactly the dimension that is skewed.

changes: ~ Accounts over 100 k followers: no fan-out
+ Their posts are merged in at read time

steps.title: Case: feeds nobody reads
body: Of everyone who follows Ana, perhaps a third opened the app this month. Fanning out to the rest fills memory with lists nobody will ever look at.

So skip them: fan out only to followers active in the last 30 days, and let everyone else’s list expire. When a lapsed user comes back, build their feed once with the pull model, cache it, and resume pushing.

callout.text: The pull path never goes away. It is how feeds are created, repaired and rebuilt — push is an optimisation layered on top of it.

changes: ~ Fan out only to recently active followers
+ Returning users: rebuilt by pull, once

steps.title: Scrolling: cursors, not page numbers
body: Alice scrolls down for more. “Page 2” would mean “skip 20, take 20” — but three new posts have arrived at the top since page 1, so she’d see three posts twice.
Use a cursor instead (see REST, RPC & GraphQL): “give me 20 posts older than post 9017”. The position is tied to a post, not to a count, so new arrivals can’t shift it.

callout.text: Time-ordered ids (Unique IDs at Scale) make this easy: “older than” is simply “id less than”.

card.title: Cursor pagination
lines: = stays put while new posts arrive

steps.title: Case: the feed cache is wiped
body: A bad deploy flushes the feed cache. Every feed is gone — and nothing of value is lost. Posts and the follow graph are the source of truth; feed lists are derived data that can be rebuilt from them.

The danger is a stampede: millions of users rebuilding by pull at the same moment. So rebuild lazily, only when a user actually opens the app; cap how many rebuilds run at once; and serve a thinner feed until the cache is warm again.

callout.text: Know which of your data is the truth and which is a convenience. You can afford to be relaxed about the second only because you are strict about the first.

changes: ~ Feeds rebuilt on demand from posts + follows
~ Rebuilds throttled to protect the post store

tags.text: rebuild on open · max 500 at once

steps.title: The finished design
body:
QuestionDecisionBecause
Build feedsOn write (push)40 reads per post
CelebritiesPull, merged at read50 M writes per post
Feed entriesPost ids, cappedOne copy of each post
Idle usersNo fan-out; rebuildUnread feeds cost memory
ScrollingCursorsNew posts shift pages
A ranked feed adds one more stage — score the candidates before returning them — but the plumbing underneath is the same.

callout.text: Next up: Design a Chat System — where every message has to arrive, in order, and show up exactly once.

design-chat.title: Design a Chat System
design-chat.summary: Twenty million open connections, and a promise: every message arrives, in order, exactly once.

goals.text: Size connections as well as messages
Groups, presence and a gateway failure

steps.title: The brief: a chat app
body: Third design: one-to-one and small-group chat, like WhatsApp or Messenger. Messages arrive instantly when the other person is online, wait for them when they aren’t, and show up on all of their devices.

What matters most is trust: no message may be lost, messages must appear in order, and each one exactly once. Speed matters too — under 200 ms when both people are online — but never at the cost of those three.

callout.text: Compare the last design. The feed could be late and approximate; chat has to be complete and ordered. Same building blocks, opposite priorities.

card.title: Requirements
lines: send      to a person or a group
receive   at once if online, later if not
= never lost · in order · shown once
# under 200 ms when both are online

steps.title: Put numbers on it
body: 50 million people use it each day and send 40 messages each: 2 billion messages a day, about 23,000 a second — several times that at peak. Messages are small (≈ 200 bytes), but that is still 400 GB a day, around 150 TB a year.
The unusual number is connections. Chat is pushed, not polled, so every online user holds a connection open. At peak that’s 20 million of them.

callout.text: One well-tuned server can hold a few hundred thousand mostly-idle connections. Twenty million means about a hundred servers that do nothing but hold sockets.

steps.title: First draft: one server, two sockets
body: From Real-time Updates: polling wastes requests and adds delay, so each phone opens a WebSocket — one long-lived connection that the server can push down at any moment.
With a single server the rest is trivial. Alice and Bob are both connected to it; when Alice’s message arrives, the server finds Bob’s socket in its own memory and writes to it.

callout.text: Unlike everything in Stateless Services, this server is stateful: Bob’s connection lives on one particular machine. That single fact shapes the rest of the design.

steps.title: A hundred servers: where is Bob?
body: Twenty million sockets need about a hundred servers. Split the roles: gateways do nothing but hold connections, and a stateless chat service behind them holds the logic.
Now Alice is connected to gateway 1 and Bob to gateway 2. Alice’s message reaches the chat service — which has no idea which of a hundred gateways is holding Bob’s socket.

callout.text: Keep gateways dumb. Logic changes every day; if it lives behind the gateways you can deploy it without dropping twenty million connections.

changes: − The chat service can’t find Bob

steps.title: A registry of who is connected where
body: When a device connects, its gateway writes an entry into a fast in-memory store: bob → gateway 2, with a short TTL that heartbeats keep refreshing. The chat service looks Bob up and hands the message to the right gateway, which writes it to his socket.
It’s Service Discovery again, at the scale of individual users: a registry kept honest by heartbeats.

callout.text: If an entry is missing or stale, nothing breaks: Bob is treated as offline and gets the message when he next connects. Which means it needs somewhere to wait…

changes: ~ Messages are routed to the right gateway

steps.title: Write it down before you pass it on
body: So far a message exists only in memory while it travels. If a server crashes mid-delivery, it’s gone. The rule: store first, then deliver. The chat service writes each message to a durable store, and only then tells Alice “sent ✓”.
In the same step it stamps the message with the conversation’s next sequence number. Order is decided once, by the server — never by the phones’ clocks, which disagree (see CAP & Consistency).

callout.text: The store is write-heavy and always read the same way — “the latest messages of conversation X”. Partition by conversation id, sort by sequence: a wide-column store such as Cassandra or HBase — both LSM engines, see Storage Engines — fits well.

card.title: One row per message
lines: = “latest 50 of conv 88” is one range read

steps.title: Case: Bob is in a tunnel
body: Bob’s phone loses signal. His registry entry expires, so the chat service knows not to try. The message is already safe in the store, and a push notification goes out through Apple’s or Google’s service to wake his phone.

When Bob reconnects, his app says “I have conversation 88 up to #41”, and the server replies with everything after it. This sync by cursor is one mechanism for a five-second gap, a week offline, or a brand-new device.

callout.text: Live delivery is an optimisation. The real protocol is “store, then sync” — the open socket only makes the sync happen sooner.

steps.title: Case: sent twice, shown once
body: Alice hits send in a lift. The message reaches the server and is stored — but the “sent ✓” reply gets lost. Her app can’t tell, so it retries, and now the server has received the same message twice.

Fix it the way Timeouts & Retries taught: the app gives every message a unique id before sending and reuses it on every retry. The server recognises an id it has already stored and simply acknowledges again. Receiving apps discard duplicates the same way.

callout.text: At-least-once delivery plus idempotent receivers adds up to “exactly once” on the screen. The ticks are plain acknowledgements: ✓ stored by the server, ✓✓ received by the device.

changes: + Message ids generated on the device
~ A retry reuses its id → stored once

steps.title: Group chats: store once, deliver to many
body: A group message is stored once, in the group’s conversation. Then the chat service looks up the members, finds each one’s gateway in the registry, and delivers a copy to every device that is online — fan-out on write, just like the news feed.
That works well up to a few hundred members. A channel with 100,000 members is the celebrity problem again; there, apps fetch new messages when the channel is opened instead.

callout.text: Members who are offline cost nothing extra: each syncs from its own cursor when it returns.

changes: ~ One stored message → a delivery per online member

steps.title: “Online” and “typing…” play by other rules
body: Presence looks simple and is surprisingly expensive: each time someone connects or disconnects, every one of their contacts’ screens may need an update. With 20 million people coming and going, that’s a storm of tiny messages.

So treat it as ephemeral. Derive “online” from the registry’s heartbeats; send updates only to people who have that chat or contact list open right now; never store “typing…” at all. If an update is lost, the next heartbeat corrects it.

callout.text: One product, two consistency levels: messages are durable and ordered; presence is best-effort and may be seconds stale. Choosing per feature is the CAP lesson in practice.

changes: ~ Updates only to people who are looking

steps.title: Case: a gateway dies
body: Gateway 2 crashes and 200,000 sockets drop at once. No message is lost — everything was stored first — but 200,000 apps now try to reconnect in the same second, and could knock over whichever gateway they land on.

The apps reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter (Timeouts & Retries), the load balancer spreads them across the healthy gateways, each one registers its new location, and every app syncs from its cursor.

callout.text: Stateful servers fail loudly. Plan for the reconnect storm — and before a deploy, drain gateways gently instead of cutting everyone off at once.

changes: ~ Apps reconnect with backoff and jitter
~ Bob lands on gateway 1 and syncs from #43

steps.title: The finished design
body:
QuestionDecisionBecause
TransportWebSockets on dumb gatewaysServer must push; 20 M sockets
RoutingRegistry: user → gatewayConnections are stateful
DurabilityStore first, then deliverNever lose a message
Order, duplicatesServer sequence + device idsClocks and retries lie
OfflinePush + sync by cursorOne path for every gap
End-to-end encryption (Encryption & Secrets) changes what the server can read, not this architecture: it stores and forwards ciphertext.

callout.text: That’s the course. You have the building blocks and three complete designs — now pick a product you use every day and sketch how you would build it.
